name: Offensive Holding
short: A blocker grabs, hooks or tackles a defender to stop him instead of blocking with hands inside the chest; the offense loses 10 yards.
watch: Look for a defender's jersey stretched out or a rusher yanked sideways or to the ground.
deep: On passes it is marked off from the previous spot. On runs, a hold beyond the line is marked from where it happened, which can erase a long gain.
Holding by the offense in its own end zone is a safety: 2 points for the defense and they get the ball back on a free kick.
Officials look for a hold that affects the play: hooking an arm, pulling a defender off his path, or tackling him. Hands inside the frame are legal.
It is the most frequently called penalty in the NFL, which is why fans joke that holding could be called on every play.

penalty.signal: The referee grabs one wrist with the other hand, fist clenched, in front of the chest.

name: Defensive Holding
short: A defender grabs or restricts a player who does not have the ball, often a receiver in his route; 5 yards and an automatic first down.
watch: Look for a cornerback grabbing a receiver's jersey or arm as he tries to break off his route.
deep: The automatic first down is the real cost: a 5-yard flag on 3rd-and-15 still keeps the drive alive.
Holding can happen before the pass is thrown; pass interference is contact while the ball is in the air. That is often the difference between 5 yards and 40.
Detroit proposed removing the automatic first down for defensive holding and illegal contact in 2025. Owners voted it down.
If the offense completes a big play anyway, it simply declines the flag and keeps the yards.

penalty.signal: The referee grabs one wrist with the other hand, fist clenched, in front of the chest.

name: Defensive Pass Interference
short: A defender illegally blocks a receiver's chance to catch a catchable pass in the air; the offense gets the ball at the foul spot with a first down.
watch: Watch the receiver's arms: a defender grabbing, hooking or running through him before the ball arrives is the classic call.
deep: It is a spot foul with no yardage cap in the NFL, unlike college's 15-yard maximum, so one flag can be worth 40 or 50 yards.
If the foul happens in the end zone, the offense gets a first down at the 1-yard line.
It only applies to passes that cross the line of scrimmage, and not to a pass that is clearly uncatchable. Both players have an equal right to the ball.
PI calls were made reviewable for the 2019 season only, after the Rams-Saints playoff no-call; the experiment was dropped the next year.

penalty.signal: The referee pushes both open hands forward from the shoulders, palms facing out, like shoving someone.

name: Offensive Pass Interference
short: A receiver illegally pushes off or blocks a defender to get open on a pass that crosses the line of scrimmage; 10 yards from the previous spot.
watch: Look for a receiver's arm extending into the defender at the top of the route, or a receiver running into a defender instead of running his route.
deep: Pick plays are the common trap: a receiver blocking a defender more than 1 yard downfield before the pass is thrown is OPI, so rub routes are run tight to the line.
Downfield blocking is legal on screens and other passes caught behind the line of scrimmage, because the pass never crosses it.
Receivers and defenders can both hand-fight; the flag comes when one arm extension creates the separation.
If the defense also commits PI on the same play, the fouls offset and the down is replayed.

penalty.signal: The referee pushes both open hands forward from the shoulders, palms facing out, like shoving someone.

name: False Start
short: An offensive player moves in a way that imitates the snap before the ball is snapped; the play is blown dead and the offense loses 5 yards.
watch: Watch the offensive linemen in their stances right before the snap; any flinch draws a flag.
deep: It is a dead-ball foul, so there is no play and no free play; the whistle blows immediately.
Once set in a three-point stance, a lineman cannot move at all. Even a head bob or shoulder twitch counts.
Loud road stadiums create false starts; offenses use silent counts, where the center snaps on a visual cue.
In the final minute of a half it can also trigger a 10-second runoff, which can end the game.

penalty.signal: The referee rolls both forearms over each other in front of the body.

name: Offside
short: A defender is across the line of scrimmage when the ball is snapped; 5 yards, and the offense gets a free play because the flag can't hurt them.
watch: If a defender crosses early and the quarterback immediately throws deep, he knows he has a free play.
deep: Offside is a live-ball foul: the play runs, then the offense chooses the result of the play or the 5 yards.
A defender who crosses early can get back before the snap without a foul, as long as he doesn't touch anyone or draw a flinch.
Encroachment and neutral zone infraction are the dead-ball cousins: the whistle blows before the snap.
The kicking team can also be offside on kickoffs by crossing its line before the ball is kicked.

penalty.signal: The referee places both hands on the hips.

diagram.caption: Right end is past the line at the snap: flag, play continues.

name: Encroachment
short: Before the snap, a defender crosses into the neutral zone and touches an offensive player; the play is blown dead and the defense loses 5 yards.
watch: Look for a defensive lineman who jumps and bumps the offensive lineman in front of him before the ball moves.
deep: Contact is the key: crossing early and getting back with no contact is not encroachment.
It is a dead-ball foul, so unlike offside there is no free play.
If the offensive player flinches first, the flag goes on the offense as a false start instead.
Touching the ball before the snap is also encroachment.

penalty.signal: The referee places both hands on the hips.

diagram.caption: Tackle crosses and touches the guard before the snap: dead ball.

name: Neutral Zone Infraction
short: Before the snap, a defender enters the neutral zone and makes an offensive player flinch, or has a free path to the quarterback; dead ball, 5 yards.
watch: If an offensive lineman flinches but the flag is on the defense, a defender jumped first and triggered it.
deep: The neutral zone is the space between the two ends of the football, about a foot wide, that neither side may enter before the snap.
The flinch is blamed on the defender, so the offensive player is not charged with a false start.
Officials also blow it dead when a defender gets an unabated path to the quarterback, to protect the passer.
Hard counts are designed to draw exactly this foul.

penalty.signal: The referee places both hands on the hips.

diagram.caption: End jumps into the neutral zone and the tackle flinches: foul on defense.

name: Delay of Game
aka: delay of game on the offense
short: The offense doesn't snap the ball before the play clock hits zero, or a player delays the game after a play; 5 yards.
watch: Watch the play clock in the corner of the screen as it ticks under five seconds.
deep: The play clock is 40 seconds after most plays and 25 seconds after stoppages like timeouts, penalties and changes of possession.
Teams sometimes take a delay on purpose before a punt to give the punter more room, or before a long field goal they plan to punt instead.
Defenses can be flagged too, for example for slowly unpiling or not releasing the runner.
The penalty cannot be a way to save time: in the final minute it can come with a 10-second runoff.

penalty.signal: The referee folds both arms across the chest.

name: Illegal Formation
short: The offense lines up wrong at the snap, most often with fewer than seven players on the line of scrimmage; 5 yards.
watch: Count the players on the line: two receivers both standing on the line on the same side is a common tell.
deep: At least seven players must be on the line and no more than four in the backfield.
Only the two players on the ends of the line, plus backfield players, are eligible receivers. A receiver on the line outside a tight end covers him up and makes him ineligible.
At least five players on the line must wear ineligible numbers (50-79) unless a player reports a change to the referee.
Officials often warn a receiver to step back before the snap, which is why you see them pointing at players before the play.

penalty.signal: The referee rolls both forearms over each other in front of the body.

diagram.caption: Seven on the line (highlighted ends). Y and Z are off the line.

name: Illegal Shift
short: After the offense lines up, two or more players move at once and the team doesn't hold still for a full second before the snap; 5 yards.
watch: When several players change spots before the snap, watch whether everyone freezes before the ball is snapped.
deep: After a shift, all 11 players must be set for at least one second before the snap.
Illegal motion is different: that is one player moving the wrong way at the snap.
Offenses shift to force defenses to reveal coverage or get their alignment wrong, so they risk this flag often.
It is a live-ball foul, so the play runs and the flag is sorted out after.

penalty.signal: The referee sweeps both hands in a horizontal arc in front of the body.

name: Illegal Motion
short: At the snap, a player in motion is moving toward the line of scrimmage, or more than one player is moving; 5 yards.
watch: Watch the player in motion at the moment of the snap: he must be moving sideways or backward, not forward.
deep: Only one player may be in motion at the snap, and he must be a backfield player, not someone on the line.
The NFL does not allow forward motion at the snap, unlike the CFL where receivers get running starts.
Jet motion is legal because the player is running parallel to the line when the ball is snapped.
It is a live-ball foul: the play runs and the flag is sorted out after.

penalty.signal: The referee sweeps one hand in a horizontal arc in front of the body.

name: Illegal Use of Hands
short: A player uses his hands illegally, most often striking an opponent's face or neck; 10 yards on offense, 5 plus a first down on defense.
watch: Look for a pass rusher or blocker whose hand snaps up into an opponent's facemask and pushes the head back.
deep: Hands to the face is the version fans hear most, called on both linemen and pass rushers.
On defense it carries an automatic first down, so it hurts like defensive holding.
The offensive version is enforced like holding: 10 yards.
It covers other illegal hand use too, like a defender grabbing or striking a blocker's head.

penalty.signal: The referee grabs one wrist in front of the chest with the other hand open and facing forward.

rule: Rule 12, Section 1, Article 7; Rule 12, Section 1, Article 3

name: Illegal Contact
short: More than 5 yards past the line, a defender makes significant contact with a receiver before the pass is thrown; 5 yards and an automatic first down.
watch: Watch a corner who keeps jamming a receiver well past the first few yards while the quarterback is still holding the ball.
deep: Within 5 yards of the line, defenders may jam receivers. Beyond that, only incidental contact is allowed until the ball is thrown.
The restriction ends when the quarterback leaves the pocket or the ball leaves his hand; after the throw it becomes a pass interference question.
The league made it a point of emphasis in 2004 after complaints about physical coverage, and passing numbers jumped.
Detroit's 2025 proposal to remove the automatic first down for illegal contact and defensive holding failed.

penalty.signal: The referee extends one open hand forward, like a push.

name: Roughing the Passer
short: A defender hits the quarterback illegally, like late, to the head, at the knees, or landing with full body weight; 15 yards and a first down.
watch: Watch the pass rusher after the throw: two steps after the ball is gone, a hit to the helmet, or a body-slam landing are the usual flags.
deep: Protected areas: no forcible hits to the head or neck, no forcible hits at or below the knee, and no landing on the passer with most of your body weight.
A rusher gets roughly one step after the release; anything later is judged a late hit.
If the pass is completed, the 15 yards is added from the end of the play, so the offense gets both.
It is a judgment call and cannot be challenged. The 2025 replay assist expansion did not include it.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head (personal foul), then makes a throwing motion.

name: Roughing the Kicker
short: A defender slams into the kicker, punter or holder without touching the ball first; 15 yards and an automatic first down for the kicking team.
watch: After a punt, watch whether a rusher who missed the ball wipes out the punter's plant leg.
deep: Roughing is forceful contact or hitting the plant leg; lighter contact is running into the kicker, only 5 yards.
No foul if the defender touches the ball first, or if he was blocked or pushed into the kicker.
The first down often extends the drive, because the kicking team keeps the ball.
Since 2025, replay assist can pick up a roughing or running-into-the-kicker flag if video clearly shows no foul. It cannot add one.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head, then swings one leg in a kicking motion.

changed: Changed in 2025: replay assist can remove a wrongly thrown flag

name: Running Into the Kicker
short: A defender makes minor contact with the kicker or punter after the kick without hitting him hard; 5 yards and no automatic first down.
watch: Look for a rusher who brushes the punter's kicking leg as he follows through.
deep: It gives the kicking team a first down only if 5 yards is enough to reach the line to gain, like 4th-and-2.
The difference from roughing is force and target: a hard hit or hitting the plant leg is roughing.
Kickers and punters sometimes sell contact to turn a brush into a flag.
Replay assist has been allowed to wipe out a clearly wrong flag since 2025.

penalty.signal: The referee swings one leg in a kicking motion.

changed: Changed in 2025: replay assist can remove a wrongly thrown flag

name: Unnecessary Roughness
short: An excessively violent act, like a late hit, a hit out of bounds, or piling on; 15 yards, plus a first down if by the defense.
watch: Watch the whistle: a shove or hit after the runner is down or out of bounds is the classic call.
deep: It is the most common type of personal foul and applies to both teams.
The hip-drop tackle, banned in 2024, is called as unnecessary roughness.
A flagrant act can also get the player ejected. Starting in 2026 the league office can order an ejection even when no flag was thrown.
Fouls after the play are added to the result, so a 20-yard gain plus a late hit can be a 35-yard swing.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head.

name: Unsportsmanlike Conduct
short: Behavior against the spirit of the game, like taunting, abusive language, or removing a helmet on the field; 15 yards, plus a first down on defense.
watch: Watch after big plays and touchdowns, when players get in opponents' faces.
deep: Two unsportsmanlike conduct fouls in one game get a player ejected.
Fouls after a touchdown are usually enforced on the extra point or the kickoff.
The NFL loosened celebration rules in 2017, allowing group celebrations and using the ball as a prop, but celebrations aimed at an opponent still draw flags.
Players can be fined afterward even if no flag was thrown.

penalty.signal: The referee holds both arms straight out to the sides, palms down.

name: Taunting
short: A player mocks, points at, or yells at an opponent in a provoking way; 15 yards as unsportsmanlike conduct, and two in one game means ejection.
watch: Look for a player standing over a tackled opponent or pointing the ball at a defender while running in.
deep: It is a type of unsportsmanlike conduct, so the defense's version also gives the offense a first down.
The league made taunting a point of emphasis in 2021, and flags spiked early that season.
If a runner taunts before crossing the goal line, the foul is enforced from that spot and the touchdown can come off the board.
Taunting after the touchdown is enforced on the try or the kickoff instead.

penalty.signal: The referee holds both arms straight out to the sides, palms down.

name: Face Mask
short: A player grabs an opponent's face mask or helmet opening and twists, turns or pulls it; 15 yards, plus an automatic first down on the defense.
watch: Look for a tackler's hand hooked in the runner's facemask as the head gets yanked sideways.
deep: Grabbing and letting go right away with no twist or pull is not a foul. The old 5-yard incidental face mask was eliminated in 2008.
Runners can commit it too, for example a stiff-arm that grabs a tackler's mask.
Since 2025, replay assist can pick up a face mask flag if video clearly shows no grab. It still cannot add a missed face mask.
It is a personal foul, which is why the defense's version also gives a first down.

penalty.signal: The referee grabs an imaginary face mask in front of his own face and pulls down.

changed: Changed in 2025: replay assist can remove a wrongly thrown flag

name: Horse Collar Tackle
short: A tackler grabs the inside back or side of a runner's shoulder pads or jersey collar and pulls him down; 15 yards and an automatic first down.
watch: Look for a defender chasing from behind who grabs the back of the collar and yanks the runner backward.
deep: The NFL banned it in 2005 after several leg and ankle injuries, many from tackles by Cowboys safety Roy Williams.
The runner has to be pulled down for the foul; grabbing the collar without the tackle is not enough.
Since 2025, replay assist can pick up a horse collar flag if video clearly shows it was wrong.
For 2026 the league added tougher discipline for repeat horse collar, hip-drop and other player-safety fouls, including possible suspension.

penalty.signal: The referee gives the personal foul signal, one wrist striking the other above the head, and announces the foul.

changed: Changed in 2025: replay assist can remove a wrongly thrown flag

name: Intentional Grounding
short: A quarterback in the pocket throws the ball away to avoid a sack with no receiver nearby; loss of down plus 10 yards or the spot.
watch: Watch where the pass lands: in the middle of nowhere with no receiver near it, while the QB was still in the pocket, draws the flag.
deep: It is legal to throw it away if the QB is outside the tackle box and the pass reaches the line of scrimmage, even out of bounds.
Yardage: 10 yards from the previous spot, or the spot of the throw if that is worse. The down is lost either way.
If the QB throws it from his own end zone, it is a safety.
Spiking the ball to stop the clock is legal right after a snap from under center or shotgun.

penalty.yards: 10 or spot of foul, + loss of down
penalty.signal: The referee waves both arms in parallel across the body at an angle, then points to the ground.

name: Illegal Forward Pass
short: A forward pass thrown after the passer crosses the line of scrimmage, or a second forward pass on one play; 5 yards and loss of down.
watch: On a scramble, watch whether the quarterback's whole body is past the line when he throws.
deep: The passer's entire body must be beyond the line for it to be illegal; one foot on or behind is fine.
Only one forward pass is allowed per play. Backward passes (laterals) are legal at any time.
A forward pass after the ball has changed possession, like on an interception return, is also illegal.
Whether the passer was beyond the line is a fact of position, so replay can review it.

penalty.signal: The referee waves one hand behind the back, then puts both hands behind the head for loss of down.

name: Ineligible Man Downfield
short: An offensive lineman is more than 1 yard past the line of scrimmage when a pass that crosses the line is thrown; 5 yards.
watch: On play-action and RPOs, watch whether the linemen are run blocking several yards downfield when the ball is thrown.
deep: Linemen may block downfield on runs, which is why RPOs often draw this flag: the line blocks run, the QB throws.
It does not apply to passes caught behind the line, which is why linemen can release on screens.
A lineman can become eligible by reporting to the referee, who announces it to the crowd.
It is 5 yards with no loss of down, and it is not called if the pass is not thrown.

penalty.signal: The referee touches the top of his cap with one hand.

diagram.caption: Guard is 3+ yards downfield as a pass crosses the line.

name: Illegal Block in the Back
short: A player blocks an opponent from behind, above the waist, when that opponent isn't the ball carrier; 10 yards, usually from where it happened.
watch: On punt and kick returns, look for a blocker shoving a coverage player in the back as the returner runs past.
deep: It is the flag that most often wipes out a long return.
Blocking from behind below the waist is clipping, a 15-yard foul.
Contact that starts on the side of the body is legal; officials judge where the hands first land.
It is enforced from the spot of the foul on most return plays, so the return gain up to that point is kept.

penalty.signal: The referee pushes both hands forward and down, arms angled toward the ground.

name: Clipping
aka: block below the waist from behind
short: A player blocks an opponent from behind at or below the waist when that opponent isn't the ball carrier; 15 yards.
watch: Look for a blocker diving at the back of a defender's legs, especially on returns.
deep: It is treated more harshly than a block in the back because it causes knee and leg injuries.
Announcers sometimes call any block from behind clipping, but a high block from behind is the 10-yard block in the back.
It is a personal foul, so a defensive clip also gives the offense a first down.
The name dates to early football, when clipping meant cutting a player's legs out from behind.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes the back of his calf with one hand.

name: Chop Block
short: One blocker engages a defender high while a teammate hits him low, at or below the thigh; 15 yards.
watch: Look for a defender already locked up with one blocker when a second blocker dives at his knees.
deep: The NFL banned all chop blocks in 2016; before that some were legal, and zone-blocking teams used them.
It is a personal foul because the defender can't protect his knees while engaged high.
Cut blocks by a single blocker, for example on the edge on a run, can still be legal in some areas of the field.
It usually comes on running plays with double teams.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes the sides of both thighs with his hands.

name: Tripping
short: A player uses his leg or foot to trip an opponent, including the ball carrier; 10 yards, plus a first down if by the defense.
watch: Look for a blocker or tackler sticking a leg out as a player runs past.
deep: Tackling a runner by sticking out a leg is illegal, even for a defender who is beaten.
Offensive linemen can be flagged when a leg whip catches a pass rusher who is getting around them.
Since 2025, replay assist can pick up a tripping flag if video clearly shows no trip.
It is rare, only a few dozen calls a season, which is why it surprises people.

penalty.signal: The referee taps the back of one heel with the other foot, repeatedly.

changed: Changed in 2025: replay assist can remove a wrongly thrown flag

name: Too Many Men on the Field
short: A team has 12 or more players on the field when the ball is snapped, or breaks the huddle with 12; 5 yards.
watch: Watch the sideline in a hurried substitution; a player jogging off too late is the usual cause.
deep: Having 12 in the huddle is also a foul, called illegal substitution, even if the extra player leaves before the snap.
When the offense substitutes, officials hold the snap long enough for the defense to match personnel.
Coaches burn a timeout when they see the count is off, which is why you sometimes see a sudden timeout before a big play.
It is 5 yards on either side, with no automatic first down.

penalty.signal: The referee places both hands on top of his head.

name: Personal Foul
short: The umbrella name for dangerous fouls like roughing, face mask, horse collar and late hits; 15 yards, plus a first down if by the defense.
watch: When the referee announces 'personal foul', the next words say which one.
deep: Includes unnecessary roughness, roughing the passer or kicker, face mask, horse collar, hip-drop tackle, chop block, clipping and blindside block, among others.
Flagrant personal fouls can bring ejection and later fines or suspension.
Starting in 2026, the league office can consult with officials to eject a player for a flagrant act and add a penalty even if no flag was thrown.
Personal fouls after a play are enforced on top of the play's result.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head.

changed: Changed in 2026: league office can order ejections without an on-field flag

name: Lowering the Helmet
short: A player lowers his head and starts contact with his helmet against an opponent; 15 yards, and a flagrant hit can mean ejection.
watch: Look for a player dropping his head just before contact so the crown of his helmet hits first.
deep: Adopted in 2018, it applies to every player on the field, including runners and blockers, not only defenders.
It is the closest NFL rule to college targeting, but ejection is not automatic.
Helmet-to-helmet contact is not always this foul; the key is lowering the head to initiate the hit.
Players are often fined afterward even when no flag was thrown.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head and announces the foul.

name: Hit on a Defenseless Player
short: Forcible contact to the head or neck, or launching into a player who can't protect himself, like a receiver mid-catch or a sliding quarterback; 15 yards.
watch: Watch receivers stretching for passes over the middle; a safety arriving head-first as the ball arrives is the classic flag.
deep: Defenseless players include a passer, a receiver trying to catch, a sliding QB, a kick returner catching, a player already on the ground, and a player whose forward progress was stopped.
Launching means leaving your feet and driving up and forward into the head area.
Since 2025, replay assist can pick up the flag if video clearly shows the hit was legal.
It is one of the player-safety fouls given tougher repeat-offender discipline in 2026.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head and announces the foul.

changed: Changed in 2025: replay assist can remove a wrongly thrown flag

name: Leverage
short: On a field goal or extra point, a defender climbs on, or is lifted or pushed by, a teammate to reach the kick; 15 yards.
watch: On a field goal, look for a defender stepping on or being boosted by a teammate to get higher.
deep: It protects the linemen on the kicking team, who can't defend themselves from someone coming over the top.
Leaping is the related foul: a running start and jumping over the line.
A foul on a field goal try often gives the offense a first down and a shot at a touchdown instead.
It is rare, but announcers bring it up whenever a kick is blocked.

penalty.signal: No unique signal; the referee announces the foul.

name: Leaping
short: On a field goal or extra point, a defender takes a running start and jumps over the blockers to block the kick; 15 yards.
watch: On a kick, look for a defender starting a few yards back and hurdling the line.
deep: The NFL banned it in 2017 because of the risk of a jumper landing on his head.
Jumping straight up from a stance at the line to block a kick is still legal.
A foul on a field goal try often gives the offense a first down and a chance at a touchdown.
A defender who leaps and lands on blockers can also be flagged, since the rule is about protecting players on the line.

penalty.signal: No unique signal; the referee announces the foul.

name: Fair Catch Interference
short: A kicking team player touches or gets in the way of a returner who signaled for a fair catch; 15 yards from the spot of the foul.
watch: On a punt, watch whether a gunner hits the returner as the ball arrives after he waved his arm.
deep: The fair catch is awarded even if the ball is not caught.
The receiving team takes the ball after the penalty anyway, so it starts a fresh set of downs.
Kick catch interference covers the same situation without a fair catch signal.
Fair catches are not allowed on kickoffs under the dynamic kickoff, so this is a punt play.

penalty.signal: No unique signal; the referee announces the foul.

name: Kick Catch Interference
aka: interference with the opportunity to catch
short: A kicking team player gets in the way of a returner trying to catch a punt, even without a fair catch signal; 15 yards from the spot.
watch: Look for a gunner arriving at the same moment as the ball and bumping the returner.
deep: The returner is guaranteed an unobstructed chance to catch the ball in the air.
Once the ball touches the ground or a player, the protection ends and it is a live ball.
A kicking team player who is blocked into the returner is usually not flagged.
The receiving team gets the ball after the penalty, so it starts a fresh set of downs.

penalty.signal: No unique signal; the referee announces the foul.

name: Illegal Bat
aka: illegal bat of a loose ball
short: A player bats or punches a loose ball, like a fumble, toward the opponent's goal or out of the end zone; 10 yards, plus a first down if the defense did it.
watch: On a fumble near the goal line, watch for a player swatting the ball instead of falling on it.
deep: Batting a loose ball in either end zone is illegal in any direction.
In 2015, Seattle's K.J. Wright batted a Detroit fumble out of the end zone; no flag was thrown, and the league later said it should have been.
Tipping a forward pass in the air is normal and legal; this rule is about fumbles and backward passes.
The penalty is 10 yards.

penalty.signal: No unique signal; the referee announces the foul.

name: Hip-Drop Tackle
short: A tackler wraps the runner, then swivels and drops his hips and body weight onto the runner's legs at or below the knee; 15 yards.
watch: Look for a tackler from behind who spins and sits down on the runner's lower legs.
deep: Banned in 2024 after a string of ankle and knee injuries, including Mark Andrews in 2023.
It is called as unnecessary roughness, so the defense's version gives a first down.
Flags were rare in 2024, but players were fined for it after games.
In 2026 it joined the list of player-safety fouls with tougher discipline for repeat offenders.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head and announces the foul.

name: Blindside Block
short: A blocker moving toward or parallel to his own end line hits an opponent with his helmet, forearm or shoulder; 15 yards.
watch: On interceptions and long runs, look for a blocker running back toward his own goal and lighting up a defender who doesn't see him.
deep: It was added in 2018 because the hit victim can't see it coming.
Blocking that way with open hands, or just getting in the way, is still legal.
Common on turnovers and punt returns, when players are running back the other way.
In 2026 it is one of the player-safety fouls with tougher discipline for repeat offenders.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head and announces the foul.

name: Illegal Crackback
short: A receiver or back who lines up wide comes back toward the ball and blocks a defender low or in the head or neck; 15 yards.
watch: On outside runs, watch the wide receiver who cuts inside to block a linebacker or safety.
deep: Crack blocks are legal and common; the foul is hitting below the waist or to the head and neck area.
The target doesn't see it coming, which is why the rule targets how the block lands.
It is a personal foul, so it is 15 yards.
Teams use crack blocks to seal the edge on sweeps and jet motion.

penalty.signal: The referee strikes one wrist against the other above the head and announces the foul.

name: Invalid Fair Catch Signal
short: A returner's fair catch signal doesn't meet the rules, like a wave that isn't fully above the head; 5 yards from where he signaled.
watch: Watch the punt returner's arm: a proper signal is one hand held fully above the head and waved side to side.
deep: No fair catch is awarded, and the returner loses the protection a fair catch gives him.
Signals on kickoffs are not allowed at all under the dynamic kickoff.
A valid signal is one arm fully extended above the head and waved side to side.
It is enforced from the spot of the signal.

penalty.signal: No unique signal; the referee announces the foul.

name: Spot Foul
short: A penalty measured from where the foul happened, instead of from where the play started; defensive pass interference is the most famous example.
deep: Most penalties are enforced from the previous spot, where the ball was snapped.
Defensive pass interference is a pure spot foul: the ball goes where the foul happened, with no yardage cap.
On runs, offensive fouls beyond the line, like holding, are marked from the spot, so the gain before it counts.
Most return-play fouls, like a block in the back, are enforced from the spot.

name: Offsetting Penalties
short: When both teams commit fouls on the same play, the penalties cancel and the down is replayed.
deep: In the NFL, yardage doesn't matter for live-ball fouls: a 15-yard foul offsets a 5-yard foul.
Fouls after the play, like a shove after the whistle, are enforced separately and do not offset live-ball fouls.
Special rules apply when the ball changes hands, like on an interception: the team that gains the ball can keep it if it had clean hands before the change.
Because the down is replayed from the same spot, any big gain or turnover on that play is wiped out.

name: Declined Penalty
short: The team fouled against can refuse the penalty and keep the result of the play when that result is better for them.
deep: The captain or head coach tells the referee, who announces 'the penalty is declined'.
Classic case: defensive holding on a 30-yard completion; the offense declines and keeps the yards.
On 3rd down, a defense often declines an offensive holding flag after an incompletion to force a punt.
If a foul is declined, the down counts as played, so a declined flag on 3rd down can still bring up 4th down.

name: Half the Distance to the Goal
aka: half the distance to the goal line
short: If a penalty's yardage would move the ball more than halfway to the goal line, the ball moves only half the distance instead.
deep: Example: offensive holding at your own 8 would be 10 yards, so it becomes 4 yards to the 4-yard line.
It works both ways; a defensive foul at the 6 moves the ball to the 3.
A defense can foul over and over near its goal line and it keeps halving, which is why officials can award a touchdown for repeated unfair acts.
Defensive pass interference in the end zone puts the ball at the 1 regardless.

name: The Catch Rule
short: A catch needs control of the ball, two feet or another body part down in bounds, and then time to make a football move.
watch: In slow motion, watch whether the ball moves or pops loose before the receiver takes a third step or reaches for more yards.
deep: A football move means a third step, reaching the ball toward the line or goal, or holding it long enough to do so.
If the receiver loses the ball when he hits the ground before completing those steps, it is incomplete.
The 2018 rewrite removed the 'survive the ground' wording and allows slight movement of the ball as long as control is kept.
Famous calls behind the rewrite: Calvin Johnson in 2010, Dez Bryant in the 2014 playoffs, Jesse James in 2017.

name: Sideline Catch
short: Along the sideline or end line, a receiver must control the ball and get two feet, or another body part like a knee, down in bounds.
watch: Watch the receiver's toes in the replay as he drags them just inside the white line.
deep: College only requires one foot in bounds; the NFL requires two.
The white sideline itself is out of bounds, so a heel on the paint does not count.
The 'force out' rule, where officials could rule a pushed receiver would have landed in bounds, was dropped in 2008.
Whether a receiver got both feet down is reviewable, and coaches challenge it often.

name: Overtime
short: Tied after four quarters, teams play one extra period in which both teams get a possession; after that the next score wins.
deep: Regular season: one 10-minute period, each team gets two timeouts, and the game can end in a tie if still level when time runs out.
Playoffs: 15-minute periods, and they keep playing until someone wins; both teams are guaranteed a possession.
A defensive touchdown or safety on the first possession ends the game immediately.
The both-teams-possess rule came to the playoffs in 2022 after the Chiefs beat the Bills without Buffalo touching the ball, and to the regular season in 2025.
There are no coach's challenges in overtime; every review is started by the replay booth.
changed: Changed in 2025: both teams get a possession in regular-season OT

name: Coach's Challenge
short: A head coach throws a red flag to ask for a replay review of a call; each team gets two per game, plus a third if one succeeds.
watch: Look for the red flag landing on the field before the next snap.
deep: A team must have a timeout to challenge; a failed challenge costs that timeout.
Coaches can't challenge inside the final two minutes of each half or in overtime; the booth handles all reviews then.
Scoring plays and turnovers are reviewed automatically, so coaches don't need to challenge those.
Most penalties are judgment calls and can't be challenged.
Starting in 2026, a staff member the head coach names before the game may throw the flag for him.
changed: Changed in 2026: a designated staff member may throw the flag

name: Instant Replay Review
short: Officials check video to confirm or overturn a call; they change it only if the evidence is clear and obvious.
watch: When the referee goes to the sideline tablet, the final decision is being made with the league's command center in New York.
deep: Scoring plays and turnovers are reviewed automatically. In the final two minutes of each half and in overtime, the replay booth decides what gets reviewed, not the coaches.
Replay assist lets the command center quietly fix objective facts, like possession or where the ball was, without a formal stoppage.
Since 2025, replay assist can pick up wrongly thrown flags for face mask, horse collar, tripping, hits on defenseless players, and roughing or running into the kicker. It cannot add flags.
Starting in 2026, the league office can eject a player for a flagrant act and add a penalty even if no flag was thrown on the field.
changed: Changed in 2025 and 2026: more fouls in replay assist; league can eject without a flag

name: Two-Minute Warning
short: An automatic timeout when the game clock reaches 2:00 in the second and fourth quarters.
deep: If a play is running when the clock hits 2:00, the warning comes after the play.
It acts like a free extra timeout, which is why teams try to run a play just before it.
Inside two minutes, coaches can't challenge; the replay booth starts all reviews.
Regular-season overtime also has a two-minute warning.

name: Clock Rules
short: The game clock stops on incomplete passes, runners going out of bounds, scores, timeouts and changes of possession; otherwise it keeps running between plays.
deep: Unlike college, the NFL clock does not stop after a first down.
Out of bounds keeps the clock stopped until the snap only in the last two minutes of the first half and last five minutes of the game.
The play clock is 40 seconds after most plays and 25 seconds after stoppages like timeouts.
A spike stops the clock at the cost of a down; kneeling keeps it running.

name: Running Clock
short: When a play ends in bounds, the game clock keeps running while teams line up for the next snap.
deep: This is why leading teams run the ball late: each in-bounds run can burn about 40 seconds.
After a runner goes out of bounds early in the game, the clock restarts once the ball is set, not at the snap.
The NFL has no mercy-rule running clock like high school; blowouts are timed normally.
Kneel-downs in victory formation run out the last seconds this way.

name: 10-Second Runoff
short: In the final minute of either half, if a foul or other stoppage stops a running clock, 10 seconds come off the clock.
deep: It stops teams from committing a foul, like a false start, just to stop the clock.
The opponent can decline the runoff. The offending team can avoid it by using a timeout.
If the runoff would end the half, the game is over; this has ended games in the past.
It also applies after injuries with no timeouts left and after replay reversals that would have kept the clock running.

name: Timeouts
short: Each team gets three timeouts per half to stop the clock; unused first-half timeouts don't carry over.
deep: In regular-season overtime, each team gets two timeouts.
A team can't call two timeouts back to back in the same dead ball; the officials just don't grant the second one. Doing it to ice a kicker is a 15-yard foul.
Icing the kicker means calling a timeout right before the snap on a field goal to rattle him.
You need a timeout left to throw a challenge flag.

name: Kickoff (Dynamic Kickoff)
short: Starts each half and follows scores; since 2024 players line up close together and can't move until the ball lands, making returns safer and more common.
watch: Coverage players stand at the receiving team's 40 and don't run until the ball hits the ground or a player.
deep: The kicker kicks from his 35. His 10 teammates line up at the other team's 40; blockers set up in a zone at the 30 to 35.
The ball must land in the landing zone, between the 20 and the goal line. Short kicks give the receiving team the ball at its 40.
Touchback on a kick reaching the end zone in the air is the 35. A kick that lands in the landing zone then rolls in is the 20.
2026 tweaks: only five receiving players must be on the restraining line, and a loophole on kicks from the 50 was closed.

name: Touchback
short: When a kick or turnover ends in the end zone of the team receiving it, that team gets the ball at a set yard line with no return.
deep: Kickoff touchback: the 35 when the ball reaches the end zone in the air, the 20 if it landed in the landing zone first.
Punt touchback: the 20.
Interceptions and fumble recoveries downed in your own end zone are touchbacks at the 20.
A fumble by the offense that goes out of the defense's end zone is a touchback: the defense gets the ball at the 20.
changed: Changed in 2025: kickoff touchback moved to the 35

name: Onside Kick
short: A short kickoff the kicking team tries to recover; it must travel 10 yards first, and in the NFL it has to be announced beforehand.
deep: Starting in 2026 a team may declare an onside kick at any time, whether winning, losing or tied. In 2025 it had to be trailing.
There are no surprise onside kicks; the officials and the receiving team know it is coming.
The kicking team lines up in a traditional formation rather than the dynamic kickoff setup.
Success rates have been very low since the 2018 kickoff safety changes took away running starts.
changed: Changed in 2026: can be declared any time regardless of score

name: Fair Catch
short: A punt returner waves one hand above his head to promise not to run; in exchange he can't be hit, and the ball is dead where caught.
watch: Watch the returner's hand go up and wave side to side as the punt comes down.
deep: Fair catches are not allowed on kickoffs under the dynamic kickoff; this is a punt rule.
Interfering with a returner who signaled is a 15-yard penalty.
After a fair catch, a team may try a free-kick field goal from that spot, with no rush allowed. It is rarely tried.
A returner who signals and muffs the ball can't be touched while it is in the air, but the ball becomes live once it hits the ground.

name: Two-Point Conversion
short: After a touchdown, a team can run or pass from the 2-yard line for 2 points instead of kicking for 1.
deep: It succeeds a bit under half the time, which makes it close to the extra point in expected value.
If the defense takes the ball away and returns it to the other end zone, it scores 2 points.
Common charts tell teams when to go for two based on the score, like being down 8 or 14.
The NFL added it in 1994; college had it since 1958.

name: Extra Point
short: After a touchdown, a kick from a snap at the 15-yard line for 1 point, a roughly 33-yard kick.
deep: It moved back from the 2 to the 15 in 2015 to make it less automatic; success fell from about 99 percent to the mid 90s.
The defense can score 2 points by returning a blocked kick or turnover to the other end zone.
A penalty on the defense can move the ball closer, and some teams then go for two.
Scoring tries are reviewed automatically.

name: Safety
short: The defense scores 2 points by tackling a ball carrier in his own end zone, or when the offense fouls or fumbles out of its own end zone.
deep: The team that gave up the safety then kicks the ball away from its own 20, so the scoring team also gets possession.
Offensive holding and intentional grounding in your own end zone are safeties.
Teams sometimes take an intentional safety late to burn clock and punt from safer territory.
In overtime, a safety ends the game.

name: Fumble
short: A player with possession loses the ball before he is down; anyone can recover it, and the defense can return it.
deep: A fumble that goes out of bounds belongs to the team that fumbled, unless it goes out through the opponent's end zone, which is a touchback for the defense.
After the two-minute warning and on any 4th down, only the player who fumbled can advance it for the offense.
If the runner was already down by contact, there is no fumble; this is reviewable.
The Tuck Rule, now repealed, once turned apparent fumbles into incomplete passes.

name: Down by Contact
short: A runner is down when an opponent's contact makes him touch the ground with anything except his hands or feet.
deep: If nobody touched him, an NFL runner can get up and keep running after slipping. In college he would be down.
Whether the ball came out before a knee or elbow hit the ground decides fumble or no fumble, and replay reviews it.
A quarterback sliding feet first, or a player giving himself up, is down where he gives himself up.
Officials often let fumble plays run and let replay sort it out, because a whistle can't be undone.

name: Forward Progress
short: The ball is spotted at the farthest point the runner reached before being pushed back, not where he ends up after being driven backward.
deep: Officials blow the whistle when the runner's forward progress is stopped, even if he is still on his feet.
A pile pushing a runner back 3 yards doesn't cost the offense those yards.
A runner whose progress is stopped is also treated as defenseless.
It is a judgment call, and officials use it to stop plays before a player gets hurt.

name: Spot of the Ball
short: Officials place the ball where its front tip was when the runner was down or went out of bounds, which sets up the next down.
deep: It is the ball, not the player's body, that counts, which is why runners reach the ball forward.
On a run out of bounds, the spot is where the ball crossed the sideline.
Since 2025, an optical tracking system measures whether the spotted ball reached the line to gain; the officials still set the spot.
Spots near the line to gain or the goal line can be reviewed on replay.

name: First Down Measurement
short: When it's close, officials check whether the ball reached the line to gain; since 2025 the NFL measures electronically with the chains as backup.
deep: Starting in 2025, Sony's Hawk-Eye camera system measures the line to gain, replacing most chain measurements.
The 10-yard chain crew still works the sideline as a backup.
Any part of the ball reaching the line to gain is enough, so the front tip of the ball is what matters.
Officials still decide where to place the ball; the technology only measures the distance.
changed: Changed in 2025: electronic measurement, chains as backup

name: Tush Push
short: A quarterback sneak where teammates line up behind the QB and shove him forward; it is legal in 2026.
watch: Short yardage: the QB under center with two or three players tucked right behind him.
deep: Pushing the ball carrier has been legal in the NFL since 2005.
The Eagles made it famous. A 2025 proposal to ban it got 22 votes, two short of the 24 needed.
No ban was proposed for 2026, so it remains legal.
Defenses counter by timing the snap or crashing the gaps, but offside rules make jumping the snap risky.

diagram.caption: Three backs push the QB forward on a sneak.

name: Targeting (College Rule)
short: Targeting is a college football rule with automatic ejection; the NFL has no targeting rule and uses lowering the helmet and defenseless-player fouls instead.
deep: In college, targeting is 15 yards plus automatic ejection, and replay reviews every call.
The NFL's versions are lowering the helmet to initiate contact and hits on a defenseless player: both 15 yards, with ejection only for flagrant hits.
Starting in 2026, the NFL office can eject a player for a flagrant hit even if no flag was thrown.
Announcers who also call college games sometimes say targeting on NFL broadcasts; it is not an NFL penalty.

name: Tuck Rule (Repealed)
short: A repealed rule that called it an incomplete pass, not a fumble, if a quarterback lost the ball while pulling it back toward his body.
deep: Most famous in the January 2002 playoff Snow Bowl: Tom Brady's apparent fumble against the Raiders was ruled incomplete, and New England won.
The NFL repealed it in 2013.
Today, once a quarterback stops his throwing motion and starts tucking the ball, losing it is a fumble.
If his arm is still moving forward to pass when the ball comes out, it is an incomplete pass.

name: Shotgun
short: The quarterback lines up about five yards behind the center instead of directly under him, so he can see the field and start the play already set back.
watch: Look for the QB standing several yards deep with his hands out, waiting for the snap.
deep: The QB saves the three to seven step drop, so he can read the defense and throw sooner. That is why most third-and-long snaps come from the gun.
The tradeoff is the run game: the back usually takes the handoff moving sideways instead of downhill, and play-action fakes are less convincing.
Offset gun puts the back beside the QB. Where he aligns often hints at run direction, so good offenses mix in plays that go away from his side.
The snap travels farther, so a bad snap is a bigger risk, especially in wind, rain, or a loud stadium where the center snaps on a silent count.

diagram.caption: QB five yards deep, back beside him.

name: Under Center
short: The quarterback lines up directly behind the center and takes the ball hand to hand, then turns and drops back or hands off.
watch: Look for the QB's hands under the center's backside before the snap.
deep: It sells the run: the QB turns his back to the defense, so linebackers cannot see whether he is handing off, faking, or dropping to pass.
That makes play-action and bootlegs more effective. Shanahan-style offenses lean on under-center snaps for exactly this reason.
The back gets the ball running downhill toward the line, which helps inside runs, power, and outside zone.
Downside: the QB loses sight of the defense while turning, and deep drops take longer, so it is rarer on obvious passing downs.
Nearly every QB sneak, kneel-down, and goal-line push comes from under center because the exchange is quick and safe.

diagram.caption: QB takes the snap directly from the center.

name: Pistol
short: A short shotgun: the quarterback stands about four yards back and the running back lines up directly behind him instead of beside him.
watch: The back lines up directly behind the QB, who is only a few yards off the center.
deep: Created by Chris Ault at Nevada in the mid-2000s to blend shotgun passing with a downhill run game.
Because the back is straight behind the QB, he can run either direction without tipping the play by where he stands.
The QB still sees the defense like in the gun, so the pistol works well for read-option, play-action, and RPOs.
NFL teams use it as a change-up rather than a base look, often to run the ball downhill with a mobile QB.

diagram.caption: QB about four yards deep, back straight behind him.

name: I-Formation
short: The quarterback under center with a fullback and then a running back lined up straight behind him, forming a capital I.
watch: Three players stacked in a straight line behind the center: QB, fullback, running back.
deep: The fullback leads through the hole and blocks a linebacker, giving the back an extra blocker on runs like power and iso.
The tailback starts seven or eight yards deep so he can see the blocks develop and pick a lane.
Offset I moves the fullback to one side (strong I toward the tight end, weak I away), hinting at run direction.
It was the dominant NFL formation for decades. Today it shows up mostly in short yardage and with teams that still carry a fullback.
Play-action from the I is very convincing because defenses expect a run from it.

diagram.caption: QB, fullback and tailback stacked in a line.

name: Singleback
short: The quarterback under center with one running back behind him and no fullback, leaving room for more tight ends or receivers.
watch: Just one back behind the QB; tight ends or receivers fill the other spots.
deep: Ace is the classic singleback look: two tight ends on the line, one on each side, with a receiver outside each.
It balances the formation so the defense cannot tell the run side from alignment alone.
Joe Gibbs' Washington teams of the 1980s helped make one-back, two-tight-end sets an NFL staple.
With the fullback gone, the back usually runs zone schemes, and the extra tight end or receiver adds a pass threat.

diagram.caption: Ace look: one back, a tight end on each side.

name: Empty
short: Nobody lines up in the backfield with the quarterback. All five eligible players spread out as receivers.
watch: Look at the QB alone in the backfield with receivers spread across both sides.
deep: Forces the defense to show its coverage: five receivers means defenders must declare who covers whom.
The cost is protection. With no back to pick up a blitzer, the QB must get the ball out fast or identify the free rusher.
Often the running back or tight end splits out wide, creating mismatches against linebackers.
Defenses answer with pressure, betting the QB cannot beat a blitz before an unblocked rusher gets home.

diagram.caption: 3x2 empty: nobody next to or behind the QB.

name: Trips
short: Three receivers line up on the same side of the formation, with one receiver alone on the other side.
watch: Count the receivers on each side of the ball; three on one side is trips.
deep: Overloads one side, so the defense must shift coverage and often leaves the single receiver (the backside X) one-on-one.
Many offenses give their best receiver that isolated spot and throw to him if the defense rolls help to the three-man side.
Trips stresses zone coverage with three routes against two or three defenders; concepts like flood and Y-cross come from it.
Defenses answer with checks like trips-specific quarters or by pushing a safety over, which the offense then tries to read.

diagram.caption: Three receivers right, the X alone on the left.

name: Bunch
short: Three receivers line up tightly grouped, one on the line and two just behind and beside him, like a small triangle.
watch: Look for three receivers huddled within a couple yards of each other near the formation.
deep: Receivers releasing from a tight cluster create natural traffic, making man coverage hard because defenders get rubbed off.
Rubs are legal only if the receiver is not blocking a defender more than one yard past the line before the ball is touched; otherwise it is offensive pass interference.
Against zone, the three quick releases in different directions confuse who takes whom.
Defenses often answer by playing banjo or combo coverage, where defenders swap receivers based on who goes in or out.

diagram.caption: Point man on the line, two tucked behind him.

name: Stack
short: Two receivers line up one directly behind the other, so the defender cannot easily jam or cover both at the snap.
watch: Look for one receiver standing a few yards directly behind another near the sideline.
deep: The back receiver gets a free release because nobody can press him without running into the front receiver.
Their routes can split in opposite directions off the same spot, which is hard for man defenders to sort out.
Popular in the red zone and against press coverage, where getting off the line cleanly matters most.
Defenses often respond with one defender playing deep over the stack and one short, then passing receivers off.

diagram.caption: Two receivers stacked, one behind the other.

name: Heavy Set
short: A formation packed with blockers, often extra tight ends or a sixth offensive lineman, built for short-yardage and goal-line runs.
watch: Look for no wide receivers and bodies crammed near the ball; listen for 'number 68 is reporting as eligible.'
deep: The goal is to have more blockers than the defense has players in the box, so the run hits before anyone can fill the gap.
An extra offensive lineman must report as eligible to the referee if he wants to catch a pass, and the ref announces it.
Defenses answer with their own heavy package, like goal-line defense with extra linemen.
Heavy sets are also a play-action setup: defenders crash on the run and a tight end slips free in the end zone.

diagram.caption: Jumbo: a sixth lineman plus two tight ends.

name: Wildcat
short: The snap goes straight to a running back or other non-quarterback, while the real quarterback lines up out wide as a receiver.
watch: Look for the QB split out near the sideline and a back standing where the QB normally would.
deep: The runner in the backfield adds an extra blocker in effect, because the defense must account for him as a runner instead of a handoff.
Popularized in the NFL by the 2008 Dolphins, who ran it with Ronnie Brown in a win over the Patriots.
Usually paired with jet motion so the defense has two possible ball carriers going opposite ways.
Its weakness is the pass threat: if the runner cannot throw, defenses load the box and wait. Teams now use it as a surprise package.

diagram.caption: Direct snap to the back; QB flexed out wide.

name: Condensed Formation
short: Receivers line up close to the offensive line instead of near the sideline, squeezing the formation toward the middle.
watch: Receivers standing just a few yards outside the tight end instead of out by the numbers.
deep: Gives receivers room to break outside, which makes out-breaking routes and crossers harder to cover.
Puts receivers in position to crack block linebackers and safeties on outside runs.
Makes defenders line up tighter too, which can confuse coverage rules built around wide splits.
A hallmark of Shanahan-style offenses that pair outside zone with play-action.

diagram.caption: Receivers tucked in close to the line.

name: 11 Personnel
short: One running back, one tight end, and three wide receivers. It is the NFL's most common grouping by a wide margin.
watch: Count: one back, one tight end, three receivers.
deep: Personnel numbers read as running backs then tight ends; wide receivers are whatever is left of the five eligible players.
It is flexible: the tight end can block like a lineman or run routes, so the defense cannot tell run from pass.
Most defenses match it with nickel, a fifth defensive back, which lightens the box for the run game.
It can line up in 2x2, 3x1, or empty with the back split out, all without substituting.

diagram.caption: One back, one tight end, three receivers.

name: 12 Personnel
short: One running back, two tight ends, and two wide receivers. It gives the offense extra blocking while keeping pass options.
watch: Count two tight ends on the field, often one on the line and one off it.
deep: Personnel numbers read as running backs then tight ends; wide receivers are whatever is left of the five eligible players.
Tight ends force a choice: defend with base personnel and risk them in coverage, or go nickel and get run over.
Offenses with two tight ends who can both block and catch get the most out of it.
Common for play-action, because the defense sees a run-heavy look.

diagram.caption: Two tight ends, one back, two receivers.

name: 21 Personnel
short: Two running backs (usually a fullback and a tailback), one tight end, and two wide receivers. The traditional pro-style grouping.
watch: Look for two backs lined up behind the quarterback.
deep: Personnel numbers read as running backs then tight ends; wide receivers are whatever is left of the five eligible players.
The fullback gives the run game a lead blocker and gives play-action a believable run look.
Fewer NFL teams keep a true fullback now, so 21 is a tendency marker for run-first, under-center offenses.
It usually lines up in the I-formation or an offset-I, but the fullback can also motion out as a receiver.

diagram.caption: Offset I: fullback and tailback in the backfield.

name: 13 Personnel
short: One running back, three tight ends, and one wide receiver. A heavy grouping for short yardage, the goal line, or bullying a defense.
watch: Look for three tight ends and only one wide receiver on the field.
deep: Personnel numbers read as running backs then tight ends; wide receivers are whatever is left of the five eligible players.
The three tight ends outnumber the defense at the point of attack and make edge defenders fight bigger bodies.
Defenses usually respond with base or goal-line personnel, and that is when offenses call play-action to a tight end.
Tight ends can flex out or motion, so the grouping is not automatically a run.

diagram.caption: Three tight ends, one back, one receiver.

name: 10 Personnel
short: One running back, no tight ends, and four wide receivers. A spread-out, pass-first grouping.
watch: Four receivers split wide with only a back next to the QB.
deep: Personnel numbers read as running backs then tight ends; wide receivers are whatever is left of the five eligible players.
Spreads the defense from sideline to sideline and usually forces a dime package with six defensive backs.
Common in college spread offenses and in NFL two-minute drills, rarer on normal downs.
With no tight end, the line handles protection alone, so blitz pickup falls on the running back.

diagram.caption: Four receivers, one back, no tight end.

name: 22 Personnel
short: Two running backs, two tight ends, and one wide receiver. A power grouping built to run the ball.
watch: Only one wide receiver on the field, with two backs and two tight ends.
deep: Personnel numbers read as running backs then tight ends; wide receivers are whatever is left of the five eligible players.
Seen in short yardage, near the goal line, and when protecting a lead late in games.
The fullback and two tight ends give the offense up to three extra blockers at the point of attack.
Play-action off 22 personnel can catch a defense stacked with nine or ten near the line.

diagram.caption: Two backs, two tight ends, one receiver.

name: Motion
short: One player moves sideways or backward before the snap to change the formation or reveal how the defense is covering.
watch: Watch whether a defender runs across the formation with the motion player.
deep: If a defender follows the moving player across the field, it hints at man coverage; if defenders just shift over, it points to zone.
Only one player may be moving at the snap, and he cannot be moving toward the line of scrimmage.
A shift is different: several players reset, and then everyone must be still for one full second before the snap.
Motion also gives receivers a running start against press and creates extra blockers at the point of attack.

diagram.caption: The slot motions across the formation before the snap.

name: Jet Motion
short: A receiver sprints full speed across the formation just before the snap, either taking a quick handoff (jet sweep) or faking it.
watch: A receiver running flat out behind the line right as the ball is snapped.
deep: Timed so the receiver passes the QB right as the ball is snapped, giving him a running start on a sweep.
Even as a fake, it pulls linebackers and safeties sideways, opening the run or play-action the other way.
Must be moving parallel or away from the line at the snap; any forward movement is illegal motion.
Shanahan-style offenses made jet motion a weekly staple, and it spread across the league.

diagram.caption: Motion across the formation, then a jet sweep handoff.

name: Play-Action
short: The quarterback fakes a handoff to freeze the defense, then pulls the ball back and throws.
watch: Watch the linebackers take a step forward on the fake, then turn and chase.
deep: It works by making linebackers and safeties step toward the line, opening space behind them for intermediate and deep throws.
Research consistently shows play-action gains more per pass than straight drop-backs, even for teams that run poorly.
Offensive linemen often fire out like it is a run, but they cannot go downfield more than a yard before the pass or it is ineligible downfield.
Defenses fight it with eye discipline, keeping safeties reading receivers rather than the backfield.

diagram.caption: Fake to the back (dashed), then a deep shot.

name: RPO
short: A run play with a built-in pass option: the quarterback reads one defender after the snap and either hands off or throws.
watch: Watch the QB hold the ball in the back's belly while staring at a linebacker, then decide.
deep: The QB reads a conflict defender, often an overhang linebacker or safety who is responsible for both run and pass.
If that defender crashes toward the run, the QB throws where he left; if he drops into coverage, the QB hands off into a lighter box.
Linemen block the run, so NFL rules say they cannot be more than one yard downfield when a pass crossing the line is thrown.
Defenses beat RPOs with disguise, making the key defender's job unclear until after the snap, or by fitting the run with a different player.

diagram.caption: If the linebacker attacks the run, throw the slant behind him.

name: Read Option
short: The quarterback leaves one defensive end unblocked on purpose, then hands off or keeps the ball himself based on what that end does.
watch: Watch the QB and back meet at the mesh while the QB's eyes stay on the end.
deep: Reading a defender instead of blocking him frees a lineman to block someone else, giving the offense a numbers advantage.
If the end crashes down on the back, the QB pulls it and runs around him; if the end stays wide, the QB hands off.
It works best with a quarterback fast enough that defenses must respect the keep.
Defenses counter with the scrape exchange, where the end crashes and a linebacker loops outside to take the QB.
QBs who keep the ball are fair game to hit as runners, so teams limit how often a franchise QB runs it.

diagram.caption: End left unblocked; QB keeps (dashed) if he crashes.

name: Bootleg
short: After faking a handoff one way, the quarterback rolls out the other way toward the sideline to throw or run.
watch: The QB fakes to the back going one way, then comes out the other side with nobody near him.
deep: Moving the launch point away from the pass rush gives the QB an easy half-field read, usually a flat, an intermediate cross, and a deep route.
A naked bootleg means no blocker goes with him, so the backside end must bite on the fake or the QB is in trouble.
Pairs naturally with outside zone: defenders flow with the run and the QB gets outside them.
The QB can run for the first down if everyone covers the receivers, which puts the flat defender in conflict.

diagram.caption: Fake left, QB boots right with a three-level read.

name: Screen Pass
short: A short pass to a running back or receiver behind the line, with offensive linemen released in front of him to block.
watch: Linemen suddenly stop blocking and jog to one side while the QB backs up and lofts it.
deep: Linemen let pass rushers through on purpose, then leak out. The rushers run past the play as the ball goes over their heads.
Linemen may be downfield because the pass is caught behind the line of scrimmage; if it crosses the line, they can be flagged.
It punishes aggressive blitzes and teams that rush upfield without reading.
Defenses stop it with rushers who feel the linemen letting go and retreat, or with linebackers who read the screen early.

diagram.caption: Linemen release right; back sneaks out behind them.

name: Bubble Screen
short: A quick lateral throw to a slot receiver who drifts backward and outside at the snap, with other receivers blocking in front.
watch: The slot receiver backpedals and bends outside right at the snap while the outside receiver blocks the corner.
deep: Used to punish defenses that leave slot receivers uncovered or that have too many defenders in the box.
Very common as the pass half of an RPO: if the box is crowded, throw the bubble; if not, hand off.
Must be a backward pass to stay safe for linemen blocking downfield; a forward toss past the line would change the rules.
Defenses beat it with a corner or nickel who reads it instantly and attacks the outside receiver's block.

diagram.caption: Slot bubbles outside; outside receiver blocks.

name: Draw
short: A run disguised as a pass: linemen and quarterback start like it is a pass play, then the ball is handed to a back on a delay.
watch: The QB drops like he will throw, then quietly hands it to the back a beat later.
deep: Pass rushers charge upfield, linebackers drop into coverage, and the back runs into the space they vacated.
Best on obvious passing downs like third and long, or against an aggressive four-man rush.
A QB draw has the quarterback keep it himself after a pass drop.
Defenses stop it with rushers who stay in their lanes and linebackers who read the linemen's high pass sets.

diagram.caption: Line pass sets, then a delayed handoff up the middle.

name: Hail Mary
short: A long, high desperation pass into the end zone at the end of a half, with several receivers running there to jump for it.
watch: Everyone sprints to the end zone and the QB heaves it as high as he can.
deep: Named after Roger Staubach said he threw it and said a Hail Mary, on a game-winning pass to Drew Pearson in the 1975 playoffs.
Receivers bunch in the end zone with one tipper and others positioned to catch a deflection.
The QB often scrambles to buy time so everyone can get there, and a high arc gives them time to arrive.
Defenses stack defensive backs in the end zone and try to knock the ball straight down rather than tip it up.

diagram.caption: Everyone floods the end zone for one jump ball.

name: QB Sneak
short: The quarterback takes the snap under center and immediately plunges forward behind the center, usually to gain a yard or less.
watch: The QB under center and the whole line firing straight ahead on a short-yardage snap.
deep: The fastest-hitting play in football: the QB is already at the line, so the defense has almost no time to react.
Converts at a very high rate on third or fourth and one, which is why analytics favor it.
The tush push adds teammates shoving the QB from behind and has become its own rules debate.
Defenses try to get low and win the A-gaps, or jump the snap count, which risks offside.

diagram.caption: Line surges forward; QB pushes straight ahead.

name: Zone Run
short: Linemen block an area instead of a specific defender, all stepping the same direction, and the back picks whichever lane opens.
watch: Watch the whole line step in unison to one side at the snap.
deep: Each lineman asks: is someone in my playside gap? If yes, block him; if not, help double-team and climb to a linebacker.
The back reads the defense and has a rule: press the aiming point, then cut up or cut back based on how defenders flow.
Holds up well against stunts and slants because linemen block whoever shows up in their area.
Comes in two main flavors: inside zone (aim between the guard and tackle) and outside zone (stretch toward the sideline).

diagram.caption: Line steps together; back reads and cuts (dashed option).

name: Inside Zone
short: A zone run aimed between the guard and tackle, where double teams move defensive linemen and the back finds the crease.
watch: Short, hard steps by the line and a back pressing straight at the guard.
deep: Probably the most common run play in the NFL. It fits almost any formation and pairs with RPOs and read-option.
Linemen double-team the down linemen and one blocker peels off to a linebacker once he commits.
Backs think 'bang, bend, or bounce': hit the aiming point, bend back behind the double team, or bounce outside.
Defenses stop it by holding their gaps and refusing to be moved by the doubles, so the back has nowhere to cut.

diagram.caption: Doubles up front; back presses the guard-tackle gap.

name: Outside Zone
short: A zone run aimed toward the edge. The whole line moves sideways, and the back runs wide and cuts upfield when a lane opens.
watch: The line flows sideways together and the back runs parallel to the line before cutting.
deep: Linemen reach-block, trying to get their helmet to the outside of the defender and move the whole front sideways.
The back aims at the tight end's outside shoulder and makes one cut: outside if the edge is sealed, back inside if defenders overrun.
The foundation of the Shanahan system, built by Mike Shanahan and line coach Alex Gibbs with the 1990s Broncos, and carried by his coaching tree.
Everything else in that system, bootlegs and play-action, is built to look identical to it.

diagram.caption: Line reaches right; back stretches wide, cutback dashed.

name: Power
short: A gap run where the backside guard pulls across to lead through the hole while the playside linemen block down on defenders inside.
watch: Watch a guard leave his spot and run across behind the line, then turn up into the hole.
deep: Gap scheme means each lineman blocks a specific gap or man, unlike zone blocking.
Classic version: playside linemen block down, the fullback kicks out the end, and the pulling guard leads up to the linebacker.
It creates an extra blocker at the point of attack, which matters in short yardage.
Defenses beat it by spilling the pull, forcing the back to bounce wide into pursuit, or by shooting the gap the guard left.

diagram.caption: Down blocks, fullback kicks out, guard pulls through.

name: Counter
short: The back steps one way to fool the defense, then cuts back the other way behind two pulling linemen.
watch: Two linemen pull across the formation while the back takes a jab step the opposite way.
deep: Joe Gibbs' Washington teams made 'Counter Trey' famous in the 1980s with a pulling guard and tackle.
The first puller kicks out the end; the second wraps through the hole to the linebacker.
The fake step makes linebackers flow the wrong way for a split second, which is all the pullers need.
Modern offenses often run it from the gun with the QB reading an end, making it a counter read.

diagram.caption: Jab step left, then follow the guard and tackle right.

name: Toss Sweep
short: The quarterback pitches the ball to a running back heading wide, and blockers try to seal the edge so he can turn upfield.
watch: The QB flips the ball sideways to the back running toward the sideline.
deep: The pitch gets the ball to the edge faster than a handoff, which stresses defenses with slow edge players.
Vince Lombardi's Packers made the sweep famous with two pulling guards leading the way.
Wide receivers often crack block inside on linebackers or safeties to seal the edge.
Defenses beat it with an edge defender who sets a hard edge and forces the back to cut back into pursuit.

diagram.caption: Pitch to the back (dashed) as he races wide.

name: Mesh
short: Two receivers run shallow crossing routes toward each other and pass almost shoulder to shoulder, creating traffic that frees one of them.
watch: Two receivers crossing the middle about five yards deep, nearly touching as they pass.
deep: Against man coverage the crossing creates legal picks; defenders chasing receivers get caught in the wash.
Against zone, the crossers settle in open space between linebackers.
An Air Raid signature concept, often paired with corner routes outside and a back to the flat.
Receivers can run it only a yard or two apart; if one deliberately blocks a defender downfield, it is offensive pass interference.

diagram.caption: Two shallow crossers mesh underneath corner routes.

name: Smash
short: An outside receiver runs a short hitch while an inside receiver runs a corner route over the top, putting the cornerback in a bind.
watch: Watch the cornerback on that side: he has to pick the short guy or the deep guy.
deep: It is a high-low read on the cornerback: if he sits on the hitch, throw the corner; if he drops, throw the hitch.
Built to beat Cover 2, where the corner is responsible for the flat and has deep help that arrives late.
Against Cover 3 the corner can sink under the corner route, so offenses adjust with other combinations.
China and other variants swap the routes or add a pivot to fool the same defender.

diagram.caption: Hitch under, corner route over: the corner cannot guard both.

name: Four Verticals
short: Four receivers run straight downfield at once, stretching the deep defenders so one receiver ends up open in a seam or up the sideline.
watch: All four receivers sprint straight upfield at the snap.
deep: Most defenses have two or three deep defenders, so four vertical threats creates a numbers problem.
Against Cover 3, the slot receivers attack the seams between the deep middle safety and the corners.
Against Cover 2, the offense hits the hole in the middle or the seams outside the safeties.
Receivers can adjust based on coverage, sitting down in open grass if a defender stays over the top.

diagram.caption: Four vertical routes stress the deep defenders.

name: Flood
short: Three receivers attack one side of the field at three depths, deep, middle, and short, so the zone defense runs out of defenders.
watch: Three receivers running to the same sideline at different depths.
deep: Classic vs Cover 3: the corner takes the deep route, the flat defender has to choose between the middle and short routes.
Often called off a bootleg, so the QB is already moving toward the flooded side.
The middle route is usually a 12 to 15 yard out or corner, the key throw of the concept.
Defenses answer with coverage that rotates extra help to that side or by pressuring the QB off his spot.

diagram.caption: Deep, middle and flat routes all to one side.

name: Slant-Flat
short: An outside receiver runs a quick slant inside while an inner receiver or back runs to the flat, giving the quarterback a fast two-way read.
