watch: The ball comes out fast, one receiver breaking inside and one running to the sideline.
deep: The QB reads the flat defender: if he widens to the flat, throw the slant; if he sits inside, throw the flat.
A quick-game staple for beating blitzes, man coverage, and Cover 3 with a three-step drop.
A West Coast offense building block, used to gain easy yards on early downs.
Defenses take it away by pressing the slant receiver or robbing the slant with a linebacker.

diagram.caption: Slant inside, flat outside, mirrored on both sides.

name: Dagger
short: An inside receiver runs straight up the seam to pull defenders deep, and the outside receiver runs a deep in-breaking dig into the space left behind.
watch: One receiver sprints straight up the middle while another cuts across underneath him.
deep: The seam route clears the safety or occupies the middle defender, opening a window for the dig at about 15 to 18 yards.
Effective against Cover 3 and quarters, where the safety's eyes are drawn to the vertical.
The QB reads the deep middle: if the safety stays with the seam, the dig is open underneath him.
Defenses beat it with a linebacker who drops deep to rob the dig or a safety who reads through the seam.

diagram.caption: Seam clears deep; the dig comes in behind it.

name: Y-Cross
short: The Y receiver, often a tight end or slot, runs a deep crossing route all the way across the field, usually 15 to 20 yards deep.
watch: A receiver starting on one side ends up near the far sideline, 15 to 20 yards downfield.
deep: The crosser attacks the gap between underneath defenders and deep safeties, often coming open late on the far side.
Backside receivers clear out, and the front-side receiver runs a post or go to pull the safety.
A staple in Air Raid offenses and many NFL playbooks, often run from trips or with play-action.
It takes time to develop, so it depends on pass protection holding up.

diagram.caption: The Y crosses deep across the field.

name: Route Tree
short: A numbered set of standard receiver routes, like the branches of a tree, used as shorthand for play calls.
watch: On replays, watch where each receiver breaks off his vertical stem.
deep: A common version: 1 flat, 2 slant, 3 comeback, 4 curl, 5 out, 6 dig or in, 7 corner, 8 post, 9 go. Numbering varies by team.
Numbers let coaches call a whole combo quickly, like '896' meaning each receiver's route in order.
Every route stems vertically first so the defender cannot tell which branch is coming.
Route running is about selling one branch and breaking to another at full speed.

diagram.caption: The nine standard routes from one receiver.

name: Hot Route
short: A quick route a receiver switches to when the defense blitzes, so the quarterback can throw before the free rusher gets there.
watch: A blitzer comes free and the ball is already out to a receiver right where he vacated.
deep: When the defense sends more rushers than the offense can block, someone is unblocked. The ball goes to the receiver where the blitzer came from.
Some hots are built in; others the QB signals at the line after seeing the blitz look.
Sight adjust means the receiver changes his route on his own after reading the blitz.
Defenses fake blitzes and drop into coverage to bait hot throws into waiting defenders.

name: Check-Down
short: A short, safe throw to a running back or tight end underneath when the deeper receivers are covered.
watch: The QB looks deep, then dumps it to the back a few yards away.
deep: The last read in a progression; the QB moves to it after deeper options are taken away.
Taking the check-down avoids sacks and interceptions, but too many can stall drives on third and long.
Defenses sometimes concede it and rally to tackle short of the sticks.
Backs who make the first defender miss turn check-downs into big plays.

name: Audible
short: The quarterback changes the play at the line of scrimmage after seeing how the defense lines up.
watch: The QB points, yells, and players shift or reset their stance before the snap.
deep: Many plays come in with two options; 'kill kill' tells everyone to switch to the second one.
QBs audible to get a run against a light box or a better pass against a coverage look.
The helmet radio from the coach cuts off with 15 seconds left on the play clock, so the QB is on his own after that.
Code words like 'Omaha' can mean anything; teams change them so opponents cannot decode them.

name: Spread
short: An offense that lines up with three or four receivers wide, usually from shotgun, to spread defenders across the whole field.
watch: Receivers split out wide to both sidelines with the QB in the gun.
deep: Wide splits force the defense to take players out of the box, making it easier to run with fewer defenders.
Often built around RPOs, read-options, and quick throws that punish the defense for any leverage mistake.
Dominant in college football for two decades and a big influence on NFL offenses.
Defenses answer with lighter, faster personnel and with two-high safety looks that limit explosive plays.

diagram.caption: Spread: wide splits pull defenders out of the box.

name: West Coast Offense
short: An offense built on short, precise, timed passes that act like runs, with receivers catching on the move and gaining yards after the catch.
watch: Quick, rhythmic throws to receivers breaking across the field on early downs.
deep: Built by Bill Walsh, refined with the 1980s San Francisco 49ers after roots with Paul Brown's Bengals.
Timing matters: three- and five-step drops, with the ball out as the receiver breaks.
Relies on horizontal stretches like slant-flat and uses the short passing game to control the ball.
Its terminology and progression reads live on across the NFL.

name: Air Raid
short: A pass-first offense built on a small set of repeated concepts, spread formations, and quick reads, run over and over until perfected.
watch: Four-wide shotgun, quick throws, very few runs.
deep: Developed by Hal Mumme and Mike Leach in the late 1980s and 1990s, notably at Kentucky and Texas Tech.
Staple concepts: mesh, Y-cross, four verticals, and stick. Fewer plays, more reps, better execution.
Offensive linemen take wide splits to spread out the rush lanes.
Its influence runs through college football and into the NFL, where many coaches borrow its concepts and tempo.

name: No-Huddle
short: The offense skips the huddle and calls the next play at the line, speeding up the game and limiting the defense's substitutions.
watch: The offense runs straight to the line after a play and the QB calls signals without a huddle.
deep: When the offense does not substitute, the defense gets no guaranteed chance to substitute either.
Keeps tired defenders on the field and stops the defense from matching personnel.
Peyton Manning's Colts made at-the-line play-calling famous.
Also used in two-minute drills to save clock and get more snaps.

name: Quarterback
short: The offensive leader who takes the snap on nearly every play, then hands off, passes, or runs.
deep: Before the snap he checks the defense, sets protections, and can change the play.
After the snap he reads defenders in a progression to pick a target, often in under three seconds.
Mobile QBs add a run threat that forces defenses to account for an extra ball carrier.
He is the only player who communicates with the coach by helmet radio on offense.

diagram.caption: Quarterback in shotgun.

name: Running Back
short: The ball carrier who lines up in the backfield, takes handoffs, catches short passes, and blocks blitzers.
deep: Good backs read blocks and pick holes. Great ones make the first defender miss.
Pass protection often decides playing time; missing a blitz pickup gets the QB hit.
Receiving backs turn check-downs and screens into big gains.
Teams often split carries among two or three backs to keep them fresh.

diagram.caption: Running back behind the quarterback.

name: Fullback
short: A bigger back who lines up in front of the running back, mainly to lead block, and sometimes carries or catches.
deep: Clears the way on power and iso runs by blocking a linebacker in the hole.
Fewer NFL teams carry one now; tight ends often fill the role.
Can surprise defenses as a receiver out of the backfield on play-action.

diagram.caption: Fullback lined up ahead of the tailback.

name: Wide Receiver
short: A pass catcher who lines up near the sideline, runs routes, and catches passes downfield.
deep: The X, or split end, lines up on the line of scrimmage; the Z, or flanker, lines up a step back.
The flanker's spot off the line lets him move in motion and avoid press coverage.
Top receivers win with route running, speed, size, or contested catches.
Receivers also block on runs, especially crack blocks on linebackers and safeties.

diagram.caption: The X and Z receivers outside.

name: Slot Receiver
short: A receiver who lines up between the offensive line and an outside receiver, usually a step off the line.
deep: Works the middle of the field against linebackers, safeties, and nickel corners.
Has room to break both inside and outside, so quick routes and option routes suit him.
Often gets bubble screens, jet motions, and short, fast throws.
Defenses bring in a nickelback to cover him.

diagram.caption: The slot receiver inside the outside receiver.

name: Tight End
short: A hybrid player who lines up next to the offensive tackle, blocking like a lineman or running routes like a receiver.
deep: Inline, or Y, tight ends line up on the line and block more. Move tight ends and H-backs shift around.
Their dual role makes defenses guess: base personnel for the run or nickel for the pass.
Tight ends are often matched against linebackers or safeties, a mismatch for a big, fast one.
A tight end in the end zone off play-action is one of the NFL's most reliable red zone plays.

diagram.caption: Tight ends next to the right tackle.

name: Offensive Tackle
short: The two linemen on the ends of the offensive line, who block edge rushers and anchor the outside of runs.
deep: The left tackle usually faces the best pass rusher and protects a right-handed QB's blind side.
Tackles must handle speed around the edge and power rushes through them.
In the run game they reach, down block, or pull, depending on the scheme.
Top tackles are among the highest-paid non-quarterbacks.

diagram.caption: Tackles at each end of the line.

name: Guard
short: The linemen on each side of the center, who handle defensive tackles and often pull to lead runs.
deep: Face big interior rushers who try to collapse the pocket right in front of the QB.
Pulling guards run behind the line to lead the way on power, counter, and sweeps.
Double teams with the center or tackle are key to the zone run game.

diagram.caption: Guards on either side of the center.

name: Center
short: The lineman in the middle who snaps the ball to the quarterback, then blocks.
deep: Usually identifies the Mike linebacker and sets the line's protection calls.
Must snap and block in one motion, often against a nose tackle right over his head.
In shotgun, a bad snap can ruin a play; in loud stadiums centers snap on a silent count.

diagram.caption: Center in the middle of the line.

name: Defensive End
short: A defensive lineman on the outer edge of the line who rushes the passer and sets the edge on runs.
deep: In a 4-3, ends are usually the main pass rushers, lined up outside the tackles.
In a 3-4, ends are bigger players over the tackles, focused on stopping the run and freeing linebackers.
Setting the edge means forcing runs back inside to help.

diagram.caption: Defensive ends on the edges of a 4-3 line.

name: Defensive Tackle
short: A defensive lineman in the middle of the line who fights guards and centers to stop runs and push the pocket.
deep: A 3-technique lines up outside the guard and is often the best interior pass rusher.
A 1-technique lines up shaded on the center and eats double teams.
Interior pressure is fast pressure because it comes right up the middle at the QB.

diagram.caption: Defensive tackles over the guards.

name: Nose Tackle
short: The big defensive lineman lined up directly over the center, usually in a 3-4 front.
deep: His job is often to absorb double teams so the linebackers stay free.
Two-gap nose tackles control both A-gaps.
Rarely a star stat-sheet player, but a good one changes how offenses run inside.

diagram.caption: Nose tackle directly over the center.

name: Edge Rusher
short: A defender, either a defensive end or outside linebacker, who lines up on the outside of the line to rush the passer.
deep: The label covers both 4-3 ends and 3-4 outside linebackers, since the job is similar.
Wins with speed around the tackle, power through him, or counters like the spin.
Must also set the edge against runs and not let the QB escape around him.

diagram.caption: 3-4 outside linebackers as edge rushers.

name: Linebacker
short: Defenders who line up behind the defensive line, stopping runs, covering short passes, and sometimes blitzing.
deep: In a 4-3 they are the Will (weak side), Mike (middle), and Sam (strong side, toward the tight end).
A 3-4 has two inside linebackers and two outside linebackers who mainly rush.
Modern linebackers must cover tight ends and backs, not just tackle runners.

diagram.caption: Will, Mike and Sam in a 4-3.

name: Mike Linebacker
short: The middle linebacker, often the defensive play-caller who relays the call and adjusts the front.
deep: Usually wears the green-dot helmet with the coach-to-player radio.
Offenses name a Mike before the snap to set protections, which may not be the actual middle linebacker.
Needs to diagnose run or pass quickly and fill the right gap.

diagram.caption: The Mike in the middle.

name: Cornerback
short: Defensive backs who line up across from wide receivers near the sideline and try to stop passes.
deep: They play press, jamming the receiver at the line, or off coverage, a few yards back.
In man coverage they shadow one receiver; in zone they guard an area.
Boundary corners play the short side of the field, field corners the wide side.

diagram.caption: Cornerbacks over the outside receivers.

name: Nickelback
short: A fifth defensive back who replaces a linebacker to cover a slot receiver.
deep: Nickel is now the most common NFL defensive package because offenses play three receivers so often.
Needs quickness for slot receivers and toughness to tackle in the run game.
Often a blitzer too, coming from the slot where the QB may not see him.

diagram.caption: Nickelback over the slot receiver.

name: Safety
short: The deepest defenders, who prevent long passes and help against the run.
deep: The free safety is usually the deep middle player, reading the QB and breaking on throws.
The strong safety tends to line up closer, toward the tight end side, and supports the run.
Safety alignment before the snap, one high or two high, hints at the coverage.
Not to be confused with a safety, the two-point score.

diagram.caption: Free safety deep, strong safety closer.

name: Kicker
short: The specialist who kicks field goals, extra points, and usually kickoffs.
deep: Extra points are snapped from the 15-yard line, making them about 33-yard kicks.
The snap-to-kick time on field goals is about 1.3 seconds.
On kickoffs the kicker kicks from his own 35 under the dynamic kickoff rules.

diagram.caption: Field goal unit: kicker behind the holder.

name: Punter
short: The specialist who punts on fourth down, trying to pin the other team deep.
deep: Stands about 15 yards behind the line to get time to kick before the rush arrives.
Hang time lets coverage get downfield; directional punts keep the ball away from returners.
Often holds for field goals and extra points.

diagram.caption: Punter deep; he really stands about 15 yards back.

name: Long Snapper
short: A specialist who snaps the ball to the punter or holder on kicking plays.
deep: Punt snaps travel about 15 yards and need to arrive in about three-quarters of a second.
Defenders cannot line up directly over the snapper on field goals and extra points.
Usually one of the quietest jobs in the NFL, until a bad snap.

diagram.caption: Long snapper in the middle of the punt unit.

name: Returner
short: The player who catches kickoffs or punts and tries to run them back.
deep: On punts he can signal a fair catch by waving an arm overhead, giving up the return for protection.
Kickoff returns are more common under the dynamic kickoff rules.
Ball security matters; muffs are a common source of turnovers.

diagram.caption: Punt returner deep; distances are compressed.

name: Gunner
short: Players on the punt team who line up wide and sprint downfield to tackle the returner or down the ball.
deep: Usually double-teamed by two players on the return team, called jammers, who try to slow them down.
Gunners who beat jammers pin returners and force fair catches.
They also try to down the ball near the goal line before it goes into the end zone.

diagram.caption: Gunners sprint downfield to the returner.

name: 4-3 Defense
short: A base defense with four defensive linemen and three linebackers, built to stop the run with big bodies up front and linebackers flowing behind.
watch: Count the players with a hand in the dirt: four down linemen, with three linebackers standing about five yards off the ball.
deep: The linebackers are the Will (weak side), Mike (middle) and Sam (strong side, toward the tight end).
In the 4-3 Over the 3-technique lines up toward the tight end; in the 4-3 Under the line shifts away and the Sam often walks up on the line.
Most 4-3 teams play one-gap: each lineman attacks a single gap, which favors quick, penetrating tackles over huge space-eaters.
Offenses use three receivers on most snaps, so true 4-3 base is on the field far less than nickel. Teams still say '4-3' to describe their front principles.

diagram.caption: 4-3 Over: four linemen, Will-Mike-Sam linebackers behind.

name: 3-4 Defense
short: A base defense with three down linemen and four linebackers; the two outside linebackers are usually the team's main pass rushers.
watch: Look for a big nose tackle over the center, two ends on the tackles, and stand-up rushers on each edge.
deep: Traditional 3-4 linemen two-gap: they take on a blocker head-up and control the gaps on both sides, freeing linebackers to make tackles.
The nose tackle is the anchor; if he can't hold up against the center and a guard, runs leak up the middle.
Four linebackers make rushers hard to count: any of them can blitz or drop, which is why 3-4 teams lean on disguise.
Modern 3-4 teams often play one-gap with 4i or 5-technique ends, and on passing downs they become a 2-4-5 nickel with two down linemen.

diagram.caption: Three down linemen, four linebackers; OLBs rush off the edges.

name: Nickel Defense
short: A defense with five defensive backs, swapping a linebacker for an extra cornerback (the nickelback) to cover a third receiver. The NFL's most-used defense.
watch: Find the defender over the slot receiver; if he's a defensive back rather than a linebacker, it's nickel.
deep: Named because five defensive backs is like a nickel (five cents). The usual shape is 4-2-5: four linemen, two linebackers, five DBs.
Offenses in 11 personnel (three receivers) force it; nickel is on the field for well over half of NFL defensive snaps.
The trade-off is run defense: the nickelback is smaller than a linebacker, so offenses run at him or motion a tight end to his side.
Big nickel uses a third safety instead of a corner as the fifth DB, for more size against the run.

diagram.caption: 4-2-5 nickel: the nickelback (NB) covers the slot receiver.

name: Dime Defense
short: Six defensive backs on the field, usually on obvious passing downs like 3rd-and-long, with only one linebacker or even none.
watch: On 3rd-and-long, count defensive backs; six means dime, often with a DB standing where a linebacker would be.
deep: The sixth DB is the 'dime' back (two nickels make a dime). Common shapes are 4-1-6 and 3-2-6.
Better coverage speed, worse run defense; offenses answer with draws and runs when they see dime on third-and-medium.
Some teams go to a seven-DB 'dollar' or 'quarter' package for Hail Mary and end-of-half situations.

diagram.caption: 4-1-6 dime: an extra DB replaces the second linebacker.

name: Big Nickel
short: A nickel defense where the fifth defensive back is a safety instead of a cornerback, for more size and tackling against the run.
watch: Three safeties on the field, one lined up where a nickel corner or linebacker would be.
deep: Used against 12 personnel or run-heavy offenses that still spread the field with receivers.
The third safety can play near the line like a linebacker or drop deep, which helps disguise the coverage.
It became more common as offenses ran from three-receiver sets to punish smaller nickel corners.

name: 46 Defense
short: An aggressive front that crowds eight defenders near the line and covers the center and both guards, built to overwhelm blocking.
watch: Linemen over the center and both guards, two linebackers on the line toward the tight end, and a safety down in the box.
deep: Buddy Ryan made it famous with the 1985 Bears; the name comes from safety Doug Plank's jersey number.
Covering the center and both guards takes away easy double teams and makes it hard to pull guards on gap runs.
The cost is coverage: often man across with one deep safety, which is vulnerable to quick passes and spread formations.
The idea lives on in modern bear and tite fronts that cover the three interior linemen.

diagram.caption: Center and both guards covered; eight defenders near the line.

name: Bear Front
short: A front with defenders over the center and outside both guards, so none of the three interior offensive linemen can easily double-team.
watch: A nose over the center and two linemen on the outside shoulders of the guards, with edge rushers wider.
deep: Taken from the 46. Close cousins are the tite and mint fronts, where the ends play a 4i instead of a 3-technique.
Strong against inside zone and gap runs because every interior blocker has a defender on him.
Offenses respond with outside runs and quick perimeter throws, since the front is squeezed inside.
Many college and NFL defenses use tite or bear looks as their base answer to spread running games.

diagram.caption: Bear: center and both guards covered, no easy double teams.

name: Odd Front
short: A front with a defensive lineman head-up on the center, usually with three down linemen, like the 3-4.
watch: Look for a nose tackle lined up nose-to-nose with the center.
deep: The nose splits both A gaps; he can two-gap or slant to one side.
Modern odd fronts often use a 'tite' alignment (4i, 0, 4i) to wall off the inside and force runs outside to waiting linebackers.
Standing linebackers can rush or drop, so odd fronts make the fourth and fifth rushers hard to identify.
Against odd fronts the center can't climb to a linebacker freely, which complicates inside zone blocking.

diagram.caption: Tite odd front: nose on the center, ends in 4i.

name: Even Front
short: A front with no lineman directly over the center, usually four down linemen split around him, like the 4-3.
watch: Two defensive tackles on or near the guards with nobody head-up on the center.
deep: Even fronts favor one-gap penetration: each lineman shoots a gap, which is simpler and faster.
The uncovered center is free to double-team or climb to a linebacker, which offenses use on inside runs.
Most nickel fronts are even (four down linemen), so even fronts dominate snap counts today.

diagram.caption: Even front: center uncovered, tackles over the guards.

name: Wide 9
short: Defensive ends line up far outside, wider than the tight end, to get a running start on the pass rush around the edge.
watch: Defensive ends lined up several yards outside the tackle or tight end, often in a sprinter's stance.
deep: Popularized by defensive line coach Jim Washburn; it trades run defense for speed rush.
The big space between the end and the tackles must be filled by linebackers, so they need to be fast and disciplined.
Offenses attack it with inside runs, draws and screens that let the ends rush themselves past the play.
Usually paired with 3-technique tackles, so four linemen attack single gaps upfield.

diagram.caption: Ends start wide and arc around the edge at the QB.

name: Goal Line Defense
short: A heavy defense for the last yard or two before the end zone, with extra linemen and linebackers to stop short runs.
watch: Six or more defenders with a hand on the ground, only a couple of defensive backs, everyone bunched tight.
deep: Common shapes are 6-2, 5-3 and 6-3-2; players get low to win leverage against blockers.
Defenders shoot gaps to create negative plays, since one unfilled gap is a touchdown.
Offenses counter with play-action and bootlegs to tight ends, because the defense has few coverage players.

diagram.caption: 6-3-2 goal line: every gap has a body in it.

name: Cover 0
short: Pure man-to-man with no deep safety, paired with an all-out blitz; every receiver is covered one-on-one and everyone else rushes.
watch: No safeties deep at all, defenders pressed on every receiver, and linebackers or safeties creeping toward the line.
deep: It sends six or more rushers so someone gets a free run at the quarterback if the offense can't block them all.
The risk is total: any missed tackle or beaten corner can be a touchdown, since nobody is behind the play.
Offenses beat it with quick throws, slants and hot routes, or by keeping extra blockers in for a max-protect shot downfield.
Most common near the goal line and on must-have third downs, where the deep field matters less.

diagram.caption: Six rush, five in man coverage, nobody deep.

name: Cover 1
short: Man-to-man coverage with one free safety deep in the middle as a safety net, often with one extra defender lurking underneath.
watch: One safety deep in the middle of the field, corners tight on receivers, and defenders turning to chase their man at the snap.
deep: The spare underneath defender (the 'rat' or 'robber') reads the quarterback and jumps crossers, or he can blitz or spy instead.
It is the classic man coverage: tight on timing routes, but vulnerable to receivers who win one-on-one or to rub routes like mesh.
Crossing routes hurt because defenders chase across the field; offenses use bunch and stack sets to create traffic.
Pre-snap tell: a single-high safety plus defenders aligned inside of each receiver.

diagram.caption: Man coverage with one free safety deep.

name: Cover 2
short: Two safeties each guard a deep half of the field while five defenders cover short zones, with corners squatting on the flats.
watch: Pre-snap, two safeties deep, one over each hash or wider, with corners close to the line outside the receivers.
deep: Corners jam outside receivers, funnel them inside, then sit in the flat, which makes quick outside throws tough.
The holes are the deep middle between the safeties and the sideline spot between corner and safety, often called the 'honey hole.'
Offenses attack with four verticals, the smash concept (corner route over a hitch) and seam routes that split the safeties.
Strong against short passes and outside runs; weak when a safety has to help on the run and leaves his deep half open.

diagram.caption: Two deep halves, five short zones underneath.

name: Tampa 2
short: Cover 2 with a twist: the middle linebacker sprints deep down the middle to plug the hole between the two safeties.
watch: Watch the middle linebacker at the snap; in Tampa 2 he turns and runs straight downfield.
deep: Popularized by Tony Dungy and Monte Kiffin with the 1990s Buccaneers; it needs a fast middle linebacker who can run with a tight end.
It turns Cover 2 into a three-deep look after the snap while still showing two safeties pre-snap.
Weak spots are the deep sideline holes between corner and safety, and the short middle the Mike vacates as he runs.
It depends on a four-man rush getting home without blitz help, since seven players drop.

diagram.caption: Mike runs to the deep middle between the two safeties.

name: Cover 3
short: Three defenders each take a deep third of the field, usually both corners and one safety, while four others cover short zones.
watch: One safety deep in the middle, corners backpedaling at the snap, and the other safety creeping down toward the box.
deep: With the other safety rotated down, the defense gets an eighth player near the box, which is why it has long been a base call.
Its weak spots are the seams and flats: four underneath defenders can't cover five short zones, and four verticals stress three deep.
Variants: Sky (safety takes the flat), Cloud (corner takes the flat) and Buzz (safety plays a hook zone).
Modern Cover 3 is often match coverage, turning into man on receivers who stay in a defender's area.

diagram.caption: Three deep thirds, four short zones underneath.

name: Cover 4
short: Four defenders each take a deep quarter of the field to keep everything in front, while three players cover short zones.
watch: Two safeties deep but closer to the line than in Cover 2, with corners playing well off the receivers.
deep: Built to stop deep passes; a common call on long-yardage downs and at the end of halves.
In pure spot-drop form, short throws underneath are open, so the defense expects to allow completions and make tackles.
Most NFL Cover 4 is really Quarters, a pattern-matching version where safeties read the slot receiver and help against the run.

diagram.caption: Four deep quarters, three short zones.

name: Quarters
short: A pattern-reading version of Cover 4 where safeties watch the slot receiver: they help on deep routes or charge downhill to stop the run.
watch: Safeties about 8-10 yards deep over the tackles, eyes on the slot receiver and tight end, not the quarterback.
deep: Each safety reads the #2 receiver (second from the sideline): if he goes vertical, the safety carries him; if he goes short or blocks, the safety helps outside or fits the run.
Corners play near-man on the outside receiver when he goes deep, which frees both safeties to act like extra run defenders.
That combination, lots of run support while staying two-high, is why Quarters is popular against balanced offenses.
It struggles with routes that stress the safety's read, like #2 running vertical to hold him while #1 cuts inside behind.

diagram.caption: Safeties read #2: carry him deep, or help outside.

name: Cover 5 (2-Man)
short: Man coverage underneath with two deep safeties splitting the field, so defenders can play tight on receivers knowing help is over the top.
watch: Two deep safeties plus corners and linebackers turning their backs to the quarterback to trail receivers.
deep: Underneath defenders play 'trail' technique, sitting on the receiver's hip, because the safeties protect against the deep ball.
Strong against intermediate routes on third-and-medium, where it is a common call.
Weak spots: quarterback scrambles, since defenders have their backs turned, and crossing routes that pull away from trailing defenders.

diagram.caption: Five in trail man, two safeties split the deep field.

name: Cover 6
short: A split coverage: Quarters on one side of the field and Cover 2 on the other, so the defense can treat each side differently.
watch: Two safeties at different depths: the deeper one plays a half, the shallower one plays Quarters.
deep: The name is math: Cover 4 plus Cover 2 equals 6. Coaches also call it quarter-quarter-half.
The Cover 2 half usually goes to the boundary (short side of the field) or to the side with a single receiver.
It lets a defense match the formation, putting Quarters on a receiver-heavy side while a Cover 2 corner squats on the other.

diagram.caption: Cover 2 on the left, Quarters on the right.

name: Man Coverage
short: Each defender is assigned one receiver and follows him wherever he goes, rather than guarding an area of the field.
watch: Watch motion: if a defender runs across the formation with the moving player, it's likely man.
deep: Pre-snap motion is the offense's man-coverage test; defenses fight back by passing off the motion man or bumping the whole secondary over.
Strength: tight coverage on timing routes. Weakness: defenders have their backs to the ball, so scrambles and rub routes hurt.
Common forms are Cover 0 (no help), Cover 1 (one deep safety) and 2-Man (two deep safeties).
Offenses beat it with picks and rubs (mesh, bunch), double moves, and receivers who separate at the top of routes.

diagram.caption: Each defender (dashed) shadows one receiver's route.

name: Zone Coverage
short: Defenders guard areas of the field instead of specific players, watching the quarterback and breaking on the ball when it's thrown.
watch: At the snap, zone defenders turn to face the quarterback and drop to spots instead of turning to run with a receiver.
deep: Zones keep eyes on the quarterback, which helps defenders react to throws, rally to tackle, and limit big plays.
The weak spots are the seams between zones and 'flooding' one zone with two receivers so a single defender can't cover both.
Offenses attack with flood and smash concepts and by sitting receivers down in soft spots between defenders.
Most NFL zone today is match zone: it starts as zone but converts to man on receivers who stay in a defender's area.

diagram.caption: Each defender drops to an area and reads the QB.

name: Press Coverage
short: A cornerback lines up right on the receiver at the line and tries to jam or disrupt his release to throw off the route's timing.
watch: Corners within a yard or two of the receiver, square and low, rather than several yards off.
deep: Contact is legal within five yards of the line of scrimmage; beyond that it becomes illegal contact.
Press takes away quick throws, but if the receiver wins the release, the corner is beaten with no cushion to recover.
Techniques vary: a hard jam, a patient 'catch' technique, or 'press bail' where the corner shows press then backpedals at the snap.
Offenses fight press with stack and bunch alignments, motion, and back-shoulder throws.

diagram.caption: Corners start on the receivers' noses and mirror the release.

name: Off Coverage
short: Cornerbacks line up several yards away from the receiver, giving a cushion so they can see the play and stay on top of deep routes.
watch: A 7-10 yard gap between the corner and the receiver before the snap, with the corner backpedaling at the snap.
deep: The cushion protects against the deep ball and lets the corner read the quarterback, which is why zone coverages often use it.
It concedes quick throws: hitches, quick outs and bubble screens are the standard answers to soft corners.
Off-man exists too: the corner is still assigned one receiver but starts deeper and drives on the route break.

diagram.caption: Soft corners give a cushion; the hitch is there.

name: Bracket Coverage
short: Two defenders double-cover one receiver, one underneath and one over the top, to take away the offense's best target.
watch: A corner playing tight underneath a star receiver with a safety shaded directly over the top of him.
deep: Common versions: 'under and over' (corner low, safety high) and 'in and out' (one takes inside routes, one takes outside).
Brackets are called by name against elite receivers; the cost is fewer defenders elsewhere, often leaving others one-on-one.
Offenses respond by moving the star around the formation and throwing to whoever gets single coverage.

diagram.caption: Corner under, safety over: two defenders on Z.

name: Robber
short: A defender, usually a safety, drops into the short-to-middle area to read the quarterback and jump throws over the middle.
watch: A safety who starts deep and then sinks toward the middle at the snap, eyes on the quarterback.
deep: Cover 1 Robber and Cover 3 Robber are common; the robber sits around 10-12 yards deep in the middle, taking away digs and crossers.
The robber often starts in a two-high look and rotates down late, so the quarterback thinks the middle is open.
The 'rat' or 'hole' player is the same idea closer to the line; broadcasters use the terms loosely.
Quarterbacks beat it by holding the robber with their eyes, then throwing behind or away from him.

diagram.caption: Two-high look; one safety spins deep, the other robs the middle.

name: Match Coverage
short: Zone coverage that turns into man-to-man once receivers' routes declare, so each defender 'matches' whoever enters his area.
watch: Defenders start in a zone look but end up running step for step with receivers on deeper routes.
deep: Rules are based on receiver numbers counted from the sideline in: #1, #2, #3.
Example: in Cover 3 match, the corner carries #1 man if he goes deep, and the curl-flat defender carries #2 up the seam.
It fixes classic zone weaknesses like four verticals, since vertical routes get carried instead of handed off.
The cost is complexity: every defender must read the same way, and one miscommunication leaves a receiver wide open.

diagram.caption: Cover 3 match: the seam and out routes get carried man.

name: Prevent Defense
short: An ultra-soft defense used late in halves: few rushers and many deep defenders, allowing short gains but preventing the big play.
watch: Only three or four rushers and defenders starting 15-20 yards off the ball late in a half.
deep: The goal is to keep everything in front and make the offense burn clock with short completions and tackles in bounds.
The old line is that 'the only thing prevent prevents is winning,' because offenses can march down the field in chunks.
Defenders try to tackle receivers in bounds to keep the clock running, and they guard the sidelines and end zone.

diagram.caption: Three rush, eight drop deep: short stuff is allowed.

name: Two-High Safeties
short: A pre-snap look with two safeties deep, splitting the field, which usually means Cover 2, 4 or 6, though it can rotate at the snap.
watch: Two safeties sitting deep, roughly over the hashes or wider, before the snap.
deep: Two-high shells take away explosive passes, which is why many defenses now live in them against strong passing offenses.
The trade-off is fewer defenders near the line, so offenses see a lighter box and run more.
Broadcasters call it 'middle of the field open' because no safety sits in the deep middle.
Many defenses show two-high and rotate one safety down at the snap to play Cover 1 or Cover 3.

diagram.caption: Two safeties deep: the middle of the field is open.

name: Single-High Safety
short: A pre-snap look with just one safety deep in the middle of the field, which usually means Cover 1 or Cover 3.
watch: One safety deep in the middle, the other walked down near the line of scrimmage.
deep: With one safety deep, the defense can add an eighth defender near the box to stop the run.
Broadcasters call it 'middle of the field closed' because the deep middle is covered.
Offenses attack outside the numbers and with vertical routes that isolate the lone deep safety.

diagram.caption: One safety in the post: the middle of the field is closed.

name: Disguise
short: Showing one coverage or pressure before the snap and playing another after, to confuse the quarterback's pre-snap read.
watch: Watch the safeties right as the ball is snapped; late rotation from two deep to one deep, or the reverse, is disguise.
deep: Quarterbacks read the safety shell before the snap to guess coverage; defenses wait until the snap to rotate.
Common forms are rotating from two-high to single-high, and walking linebackers up to fake a blitz before dropping.
Offenses counter with motion, hard counts and quick snaps to force defenders to show their hand early.
Also called 'rolling' or 'spinning' the coverage.

diagram.caption: Shows two deep, then spins to Cover 3 at the snap.

name: Blitz
short: Sending more pass rushers than usual, usually five or more, by adding linebackers or defensive backs to the rush.
watch: Linebackers creeping toward the line or a safety sneaking down before the snap often signals a blitz.
deep: The trade-off: more rushers means fewer coverage players, so a blitz that doesn't get home can give up big plays.
Offenses answer with hot routes, quick throws, screens, and keeping backs and tight ends in to block.
A zero blitz sends everyone and plays Cover 0; most blitzes keep at least one safety deep.
Blitz rate is a stat broadcasters cite often; some coordinators rarely blitz and trust four-man rushes, others live on pressure.

diagram.caption: Both linebackers blitz the A gaps: six rushers.

name: Zone Blitz
short: A blitz where a defensive lineman drops into coverage while linebackers or defensive backs rush, so pressure comes from unexpected spots.
watch: A defensive end dropping back into a short zone at the snap while a linebacker or nickelback rushes.
deep: Popularized by Dick LeBeau starting in the late 1980s; the rush usually has five players, but the coverage behind stays zone.
It confuses blocking assignments and the quarterback's hot reads, since the expected blitz lane is filled by a dropping lineman.
The usual shell is three deep and three underneath; today most coaches call it a fire zone.
Weakness: a big lineman in coverage can be targeted if the quarterback finds him.

diagram.caption: End drops, Will and nickel rush: 5 rush, 3 under, 3 deep.

name: Fire Zone
short: The standard zone blitz: five rushers, three deep defenders and three underneath defenders.
watch: Five rushers, with corners bailing deep and a lineman or safety dropping to a short zone.
deep: The three underneath players cover 'seam-to-flat' on each side and the 'hook' in the middle, and are taught to wall off seam routes.
Fire zones are safer than man blitzes because every coverage defender still sees the ball.
Offenses target the soft spots: quick hitches in front of the deep thirds, and the seams if underneath defenders don't get width.
Blitzers can come from anywhere: slot corners, safeties, inside linebackers, while a lineman drops.

diagram.caption: Mike and safety rush, end drops: 5 rush, 3 under, 3 deep.

name: Simulated Pressure
short: A pressure that looks like a blitz but sends only four rushers, including an unexpected one, while a lineman drops into coverage.
watch: Lots of defenders at the line before the snap, then only four come, and one of them is a linebacker or DB.
deep: The goal is to confuse the offensive line's protection so a rusher comes free, without giving up coverage players.
Seven players still cover, so the quarterback's hot throws are often met by a lineman or linebacker sitting in the throwing lane.
A creeper is a type of sim pressure; the terms overlap and coaches use them differently.
Sim pressures became a defining feature of NFL defenses in the 2020s as teams sought pressure without leaving receivers one-on-one.

diagram.caption: Double-A look, but only four rush; the end drops.

name: Creeper
short: A four-man pressure where a linebacker or defensive back rushes and a defensive lineman drops into coverage, keeping seven in coverage.
watch: A linebacker or nickel rushing while a lineman next to him backs off into coverage.
deep: The rusher 'creeps' in from an unexpected spot, replacing the lineman who drops.
Unlike a fire zone, it adds no extra rusher, so seven players cover, often in a three-deep, four-under shell.
It attacks protection rules: the line blocks the rushers it expects, and the replacement rusher comes free or gets a running back.

name: Stunt
short: A pre-planned move where defensive linemen slant, cross or loop instead of rushing straight, to confuse blockers and create free lanes.
watch: Linemen angling sideways at the snap instead of charging straight at the man in front of them.
deep: Stunts can be for the run (slants that knife into gaps) or the pass (games that exploit pass protection).
Slanting the whole line one way can blow up zone runs, but a cutback lane opens behind it if the runner sees it.
Broadcasters use stunt and twist interchangeably; strictly, a twist is a two-man crossing game on the pass rush.
Offensive lines beat stunts by passing rushers off cleanly, which takes chemistry and communication.

diagram.caption: Slant stunt: every lineman angles one gap to his right.

name: Twist
short: Two pass rushers swap lanes: one crashes inside to occupy blockers, the other loops around behind him into the space he vacated.
watch: A defensive end crashing hard inside while the tackle next to him loops around outside.
deep: Names describe who goes first: in an E-T twist the end crashes first and the tackle loops; in a T-E the tackle goes first.
The crasher's job is to pick (occupy) two blockers; the looper wins if the blockers don't pass him off.
Twists work best against aggressive linemen and on long-yardage downs, when blockers set deep expecting a speed rush.
The looper is often the better pass rusher, since he gets the free lane.

diagram.caption: E-T twist: end crashes inside, tackle loops outside.

name: QB Spy
short: A defender, often a linebacker, shadows the quarterback and tackles him if he scrambles, instead of rushing or covering.
watch: A linebacker sitting 5-7 yards deep in the middle who neither drops nor rushes, but mirrors the quarterback's movement.
deep: Used against mobile quarterbacks, especially on third downs where a scramble can move the chains.
The cost is one fewer rusher or cover player; offenses test it with routes that drag the spy's eyes or with designed runs.
In a 'rush spy' the defender rushes only if the quarterback stays in the pocket.
The spy needs speed; teams often use a safety or quick linebacker.

diagram.caption: The Mike mirrors the quarterback instead of covering.

name: Double A-Gap Pressure
short: Two linebackers stand in both A gaps right before the snap, threatening an interior blitz and forcing the offense to account for both.
watch: Two linebackers standing right over the center, one on each side, just before the snap.
deep: It stresses the center and running back in protection: if both come, someone may be unblocked straight up the middle.
Often one or neither rushes; it's a staple tool for simulated pressure and confusing protection calls.
The quarterback must identify it and adjust protection, or throw hot to where the blitzers came from.

name: Setting the Edge
short: Keeping runs from getting outside by having the end-most defender hold his ground and force the ball back inside to the pursuit.
watch: The outside defender squaring up a blocker without getting pushed wide, forcing the runner to cut back inside.
deep: Every run defense needs a 'force' player on each side; if the edge is lost, outside runs go for big gains.
It is usually the defensive end's or outside linebacker's job, sometimes a safety or corner in certain coverages.
Outside zone attacks edge setters: if he gets hooked (blocked from the outside), the run bounces around him.
Compare spill-and-kill, where the edge player crashes inside to force the ball outside to faster defenders.

name: One-Gap vs Two-Gap
short: One-gap linemen attack a single gap; two-gap linemen take on a blocker head-up and control the gaps on both sides of him.
watch: Two-gappers stand up the blocker and read the play; one-gappers shoot into a gap at the snap.
deep: One-gap schemes are aggressive and create penetration, which suits quick pass rushers.
Two-gap schemes read, then react; they're slower but sturdy against the run and keep blockers off linebackers.
Classic 3-4 fronts were built on two-gapping; most NFL fronts today are mostly one-gap with some two-gap calls.

name: Technique Numbers
short: A numbering system for where a defensive lineman lines up relative to the offensive linemen, like 0 over the center or 3 outside a guard.
watch: When an announcer says '3-technique,' find the defensive tackle on the outside shoulder of a guard.
deep: Even numbers (0, 2, 4) are head-up on a blocker; odd numbers (1, 3, 5) are on a blocker's outside shoulder.
An 'i' means inside shoulder: a 2i sits on the guard's inside shoulder, a 4i on the tackle's inside shoulder.
Near the tight end conventions vary; most commonly 7 is his inside shoulder, 6 head-up, and 9 outside him.
The system is usually credited to Bum Phillips. The numbers mirror on both sides of the center.
Gaps use letters instead: A (center-guard), B (guard-tackle), C (outside the tackle), D (outside the tight end).

diagram.caption: Gaps lettered on the left, techniques numbered on the right; both mirror.

name: A Gap
short: The space between the center and either guard. It's the shortest path to the quarterback, so blitzes through it get home fastest.
watch: Linebackers standing right over the center-guard gaps before the snap are threatening an A-gap blitz.
deep: Gaps are lettered from the center out: A (center-guard), B (guard-tackle), C (outside the tackle), D (outside the tight end).
There are two A gaps, one on each side of the center; 'double A-gap' pressure puts a linebacker in each.
A-gap runs like inside zone and the QB sneak are stopped by the nose or 1-technique and the Mike linebacker.
Interior pressure bothers quarterbacks most because they can't step up to escape it.

diagram.caption: A gaps sit on each side of the center.

name: B Gap
short: The space between a guard and a tackle, one on each side. A 3-technique defensive tackle attacks this gap.
watch: A defensive tackle lined up just outside a guard is aimed at the B gap.
deep: It is the second gap out from the center; the 3-technique and blitzing linebackers are the usual B-gap attackers.
Power and counter runs often hit the B gap, with a pulling lineman leading through it.
A linebacker's B-gap blitz is a common way to test a guard and running back in pass protection.

diagram.caption: B gaps sit between each guard and tackle.

name: C Gap
short: The space just outside the offensive tackle, between him and the tight end if there is one.
watch: The lineman on the tackle's outside shoulder owns the C gap.
deep: The 5-technique end is usually responsible for the C gap.
With no tight end, the C gap is simply outside the tackle; with a tight end, it is between tackle and tight end.
Off-tackle runs attack it, and it's where edge rushers often turn the corner on the pass rush.

diagram.caption: C gaps sit outside each tackle.

name: D Gap
short: The space outside the tight end, the widest gap. It only exists as a true gap when a tight end or wing is attached to the line.
watch: The defender outside the tight end, often a stand-up outside linebacker, owns the D gap.
deep: Outside linebackers or a safety rolled down usually own the D gap.
Adding a tight end or wing creates another gap the defense must fill, one reason heavy formations stress defenses.
Beyond the D gap, run defense becomes an edge or 'force' responsibility.

diagram.caption: D gaps sit outside each tight end.

name: 0 Technique
short: A defensive lineman lined up directly over the center, usually a big nose tackle in an odd front.
watch: A lineman nose-to-nose with the center, usually the biggest player on the field.
deep: A 0-technique often two-gaps: he controls the center and fights to either A gap depending on where the run goes.
It takes a massive, strong player, because the guards can double-team him from both sides.
Pass rushing from a 0 is hard, so these players often come off the field on passing downs.

diagram.caption: 0 technique: head-up on the center.

name: 1 Technique
short: A defensive tackle lined up on the shoulder of the center, shaded toward one A gap.
watch: A defensive tackle offset just to one side of the center, not quite over the guard.
deep: Also called a shade. His job is to attack the A gap and absorb the center-guard double team.
Usually paired with a 3-technique on the other side, as in 4-3 Over and Under fronts.
It's more of a run-stuffing spot; the 3-technique gets more one-on-one pass rush chances.

diagram.caption: 1 technique: on the center's shoulder, in the A gap.

name: 3 Technique
short: A defensive tackle lined up on the outside shoulder of a guard, the classic spot for an explosive interior pass rusher.
watch: Find the defensive tackle shaded just outside a guard; that's the 3-technique.
deep: He attacks the B gap, which often earns a one-on-one with the guard since the center can't easily help.
Many of the best interior pass rushers play here; the 3-technique is the engine of one-gap 4-3 fronts.
Offenses try to double-team him or run away from him; zone runs try to wash him down the line.

diagram.caption: 3 technique: outside shoulder of the guard, in the B gap.

name: 4i Technique
short: A defensive lineman lined up on the inside shoulder of the offensive tackle, a common spot for ends in modern odd fronts.
watch: A lineman lined up between the guard and tackle but closer to the tackle.
deep: It lets a lineman squeeze the B gap while staying strong against inside runs, a key piece of the tite front.
A nose with two 4i's clogs the middle and forces runs to bounce outside to linebackers.
It's harder to rush from than a 3 or 5, because the guard and tackle can pass him back and forth.

diagram.caption: 4i technique: inside shoulder of the tackle.

name: 5 Technique
short: A defensive lineman on the outside shoulder of the offensive tackle; the classic spot for a 3-4 defensive end.
watch: Find the lineman lined up just outside the tackle's shoulder with his hand down.
deep: He usually owns the C gap and must hold up against the tackle and sometimes the tight end.
In a 3-4, the 5-tech is a big, long end who stops the run and pushes the pocket more than he racks up sacks.
In 4-3 fronts, a 5-technique end is the stronger, run-first end; speed rushers line up wider.

diagram.caption: 5 technique: outside shoulder of the tackle, in the C gap.

name: Red Zone
short: The area from the opponent's 20-yard line to the goal line, where a drive is expected to produce points.
watch: Many broadcasts shade the field or flash a graphic when the offense crosses the 20.
deep: Red zone touchdown percentage is a key efficiency stat; settling for field goals there often decides close games.
The field shrinks: less room for deep routes means tighter windows and more man coverage.
Some broadcasts also mention the 'green zone' or 'gold zone' inside the 10, but those are team terms, not official.

name: Three-and-Out
short: When an offense runs three plays, fails to get a first down, and has to punt.
deep: It's a win for the defense and gives its offense good field position and a rested defense.
Three-and-outs forced is a common defensive stat on broadcasts.
Stat definitions vary slightly; some count possessions that end in a punt after exactly three plays.

name: Pick-Six
short: An interception returned for a touchdown by the defense.
deep: It's six points because the touchdown is worth six before the extra point.
Often comes from a defender jumping a short route, like a quick out or slant, with nobody behind him.
Pick-sixes swing win probability enormously because they combine a lost possession with points for the other team.

name: Moving the Chains
short: Getting a first down. The phrase comes from the sideline crew literally moving the 10-yard chain forward.
deep: The chain crew holds two poles 10 yards apart; a new first down means the chain is reset.
Broadcasts show a yellow first-down line on screen, but the official spot is the chain on the sideline.
Offenses that consistently move the chains keep the ball, control the clock, and rest their defense.

name: The Sticks
short: The first-down marker. 'Throwing short of the sticks' means completing a pass that doesn't reach the first-down line on third down.
deep: Named after the poles the chain crew holds on the sideline.
Analysts criticize third-down throws short of the sticks because the receiver must break a tackle to convert.
Defenses on third-and-long often sit just past the sticks, daring the offense to throw underneath and tackle.

name: The Trenches
short: The battle between the offensive and defensive lines, where most games are said to be won or lost.
deep: 'Winning in the trenches' means the offensive line is opening holes and protecting, or the defensive line is getting pushback and pressure.
Line play drives both run success and sack rates, even though linemen rarely show up in box scores.
Pass rush win rate and run block win rate are modern stats that try to measure it.

name: The Pocket
short: The protected space the offensive line forms around the quarterback on a pass play.
watch: Watch the linemen form a horseshoe; the quarterback should step up into the middle of it.
deep: Tackles push rushers wide and deep, guards and center hold firm inside, creating a cup the quarterback can step into.
'Pocket presence' is a quarterback's feel for pressure: sliding and stepping up without panicking or bailing out too early.
Leaving the pocket (outside the tackle box) changes the rules for intentional grounding.

diagram.caption: Tackles push edge rushers past the quarterback; he steps up.

name: Clean Pocket
short: A pass play where the quarterback isn't pressured at all and has time and space to throw.
deep: Most quarterbacks are far more efficient from a clean pocket, so the difference between clean and pressured stats says a lot.
A clean pocket can come from great blocking, a quick release, or a defense rushing only three or four.
Defenses that can't get pressure with four often have to blitz, which weakens their coverage.

name: Collapse the Pocket
short: When pass rushers push the protection back into the quarterback so he has no room to step up and throw.
deep: Interior rushers who collapse the pocket are valuable even without sacks, because the quarterback can't step into throws.
Edge rushers flush quarterbacks forward; interior push traps them from the front.
Stunts and twists are common ways to collapse the pocket against a solid line.

name: Yards After Catch (YAC)
short: The yards a receiver gains after catching the ball, running with it until he's tackled or scores.
deep: Total yards on a completion equal air yards plus yards after catch.
Screens, slants and crossing routes produce the most YAC because receivers catch the ball already running.
YAC over expected compares a player's YAC to what similar catches typically produce, isolating his elusiveness.

name: Air Yards
short: How far the ball travels in the air past the line of scrimmage before it's caught or falls incomplete.
deep: Average depth of target (aDOT) shows how far downfield a quarterback or receiver's targets typically are.
Intended air yards count incompletions too, so they measure a quarterback's aggressiveness.
A low-aDOT offense gets efficiency from YAC; a high-aDOT offense lives on deep shots and lower completion rates.

name: EPA (Expected Points Added)
short: A measure of how much a play helped or hurt the offense's scoring chances, based on down, distance and field position before and after.
deep: Every situation (say, 1st-and-10 at your own 25) has an average number of points teams go on to score, built from years of data.
A play's EPA is expected points after minus before, so a 7-yard gain on 3rd-and-5 is worth far more than on 3rd-and-12.
EPA per play is one of the best single stats for offense or defense efficiency; quarterbacks are often ranked by EPA per dropback.
It doesn't split credit: a quarterback's EPA includes his line's blocking and his receivers' catches.

name: CPOE
short: Completion Percentage Over Expected: how often a quarterback completes passes compared with what an average passer would on the same throws.
deep: A model estimates each pass's chance of completion from factors like throw distance, receiver separation and pressure.
Positive CPOE means accuracy beyond what the throws' difficulty predicts, which strips out easy, screen-heavy completion rates.
Analysts often pair it with EPA: CPOE measures accuracy, EPA measures value.

name: Win Probability
short: The estimated chance a team wins from the current situation, based on score, time left, field position, down and distance, and timeouts.
deep: Models are built from historical games; many also factor in pregame point spreads for team strength.
Win probability added (WPA) credits the plays that swing those odds, which is why late-game plays dominate it.
A 90 percent win probability still loses one time in ten; comebacks happen more than broadcast graphics suggest.

name: Fourth-Down Decision
short: Whether to go for it, punt or kick a field goal on 4th down; broadcasts now show analytics models weighing each option's effect on win probability.
deep: Models compare win probability after a conversion, a failure, a punt and a field goal attempt, then recommend the best option.
The data showed teams punted too often in short-yardage situations, and NFL go-for-it rates rose sharply from the late 2010s on.
Models may miss context like injuries, wind, specific matchups, or the kicker's range that day.

name: Success Rate
short: The share of plays that keep an offense on schedule, usually 40% of needed yards on 1st down, 60% on 2nd, all of it on 3rd or 4th.
deep: Many analysts instead define a successful play as any play with positive EPA.
It rewards consistency; offenses with high success rates stay out of third-and-long.
Pair it with explosive play rate: success rate shows reliability, explosives show big-play ability.

name: Chunk Play
short: A play that gains a big piece of yardage in one shot, more than a routine gain but not always a home run.
deep: There is no official cutoff; many analysts use about 10 or more yards on a run and 15 or more on a pass.
'Chunk plays' flip field position quickly and make drives far more likely to score.
Defenses built to limit chunk plays play two-high safeties and keep everything in front.

name: Explosive Play
short: A long gain, commonly defined as a run of 10+ or 12+ yards or a pass of 16+ or 20+ yards, depending on who's counting.
deep: Explosive play rate is one of the strongest predictors of scoring; drives with one are far more likely to end in points.
Offenses create them with play-action, deep shots and yards after catch; defenses limit them with two-high shells.
Chunk play and explosive play are often used interchangeably on broadcasts.

name: Middle of the Field Open (MOFO)
short: A pre-snap defensive look with no safety in the deep middle of the field, usually two safeties split wide.
watch: Look for two deep safeties split toward the hashes with nobody in the deep middle.
deep: It usually signals Cover 2, Cover 4 or Cover 6, though the defense can rotate at the snap.
Quarterbacks often target the deep middle or seams against it, and offenses like to run into the lighter box.
The opposite is middle of the field closed (MOFC), with one safety in the deep middle.

name: Middle of the Field Closed (MOFC)
short: A pre-snap defensive look with a single safety in the deep middle of the field.
watch: One safety deep in the middle, the other walked down near the line.
deep: It usually signals Cover 1 or Cover 3, with the other safety often down near the box.
Offenses attack outside the numbers and with routes that pull the lone safety one way.
Defenses may show MOFC and rotate to two-high at the snap, so it's a clue, not a guarantee.

name: Garbage Time
short: The late part of a lopsided game when the result is decided, so stats pile up against soft, prevent-style defense.
deep: Analysts filter garbage time out of efficiency stats, often using a win probability cutoff.
Trailing quarterbacks can pile up yards against defenses that are simply running out the clock.
Fantasy players love it; film analysts discount it.

name: Scramble Drill
short: The rules receivers follow when the quarterback escapes the pocket: deep routes keep going, short routes come back, everyone works toward open space.
deep: Receivers typically drift in the direction the quarterback rolls and stay in his line of sight.
Scramble plays are hard to defend because coverage breaks down and defenders turn their backs in man.
Quarterbacks who create off-script plays make even good coverage fail.

name: Back-Shoulder Throw
short: A pass thrown behind a receiver running downfield, toward his back shoulder, so he stops and turns to catch it while the defender keeps running.
deep: It beats tight press or trail coverage where the defender is running with the receiver and can't see the ball.
It requires timing and trust; the receiver often has to read it late in the route.
Common near the sideline and in the red zone.

name: 50-50 Ball
short: A pass thrown into tight coverage where the receiver and defender have roughly an equal shot at catching it.
deep: Quarterbacks throw them to big, physical receivers who win at the catch point.
Analysts debate them: a great contested-catch receiver makes them better than 50-50, but they carry interception risk.
Often a deep fade or end-zone jump ball.

name: Contested Catch
short: A catch made with a defender right on the receiver, often touching or fighting for the ball.
deep: Contested catch rate is a common receiver stat; physical receivers with strong hands post high rates.
Receivers who separate well need fewer contested catches; big receivers are often built for them.
Tight coverage without interference means the receiver wins with body position and hands.

name: Catch Point
short: The moment and spot where the ball arrives and the receiver and defender fight to catch or knock it away.
deep: 'Winning at the catch point' means securing the ball through contact, often on contested throws.
Defenders are taught to play the receiver's hands at the catch point to force an incompletion.
Timing a hand punch at the catch point without early contact avoids pass interference.

name: Route Running
short: A receiver's skill at running patterns precisely, selling fakes and changing direction to get open.
deep: Great route runners vary speed, set up defenders with head and shoulder fakes, and cut sharply at the break point.
The 'release' at the line (beating press) and the 'top of the route' (the break) are where separation is won.
Receivers are often graded on how quickly they get open, not just on speed.

name: Separation
short: The distance a receiver creates from the defender covering him, how open he is when the ball arrives.
deep: Tracking data measures separation in yards at the moment of the catch or throw.
Separation comes from route running, speed, and scheme like motion, stacks and crossers.
Receivers without separation depend on contested catches; quarterbacks with accuracy can hit tighter windows.

name: Sack-Fumble
short: A sack in which the quarterback loses the ball, which is a live fumble that either team can recover.
deep: If the quarterback's arm is moving forward when the ball comes out, it's an incomplete pass, not a fumble.
Those tuck-rule style calls are frequently reviewed.
A strip-sack is the version where the defender deliberately knocks the ball loose.

name: Strip-Sack
short: A sack where the rusher deliberately knocks the ball out of the quarterback's hand, causing a fumble.
deep: Rushers are taught to swipe at the ball as they arrive, often from the quarterback's blind side.
Strip-sacks are among the most valuable defensive plays because they can end drives and flip field position at once.
Quarterbacks protect against them by keeping two hands on the ball in the pocket.

name: Coffin Corner Punt
short: A punt aimed to go out of bounds near the pylon inside the 10-yard line, pinning the other team deep without risking a touchback.
deep: The ball is spotted where it crossed the sideline, so a good one can pin the offense inside the 5.
Punters today often prefer high, spinning punts that the coverage team downs, but the angled punt remains a tool.
If it goes into the end zone, it's a touchback at the 20.

name: Pooch Kick
short: A short, high, soft kick meant to land inside the 20 or in a specific spot, rather than for distance.
deep: Pooch punts come from around midfield, when a full punt would go into the end zone.
Occasionally a quarterback pooch punts on 4th down from a normal formation to surprise the return team.
Pooch kickoffs aim short of returners to change field position; current kickoff rules have changed how often they're used.

name: Squib Kick
short: A low, bouncing kickoff that's hard to field cleanly, used to avoid a long return, often late in a half.
deep: Upbacks usually field it, not the dangerous returner, so it limits big returns.
The trade-off is field position: the receiving team usually starts farther upfield than after a deep kick.
Current kickoff rules changed kickoff alignments, so how and when teams squib keeps evolving.

name: Point After (PAT)
short: The kick after a touchdown for one extra point; announcers say 'PAT' or 'point after.'
deep: The kick is snapped from the 15-yard line, making it about a 33-yard attempt.
Teams can instead run a play from the 2 for a two-point conversion.
Misses became more common after the league moved the kick back in 2015.

name: Goal to Go
short: When the line to gain is the goal line, so the down is announced as 'and goal' instead of a yardage number.
deep: The offense must score to get a new set of downs; there's no first down to earn short of the end zone.
Defenses shift to goal line or heavy packages as the distance shrinks.
Penalties can make it 'first and goal' again only if they carry an automatic first down.

name: Turnover on Downs
short: When an offense goes for it on 4th down and fails, the other team takes over at that spot.
deep: It counts as a failed possession but not as a turnover in most turnover stats.
The analytics shift toward going for it means more of these, but more successful conversions too.
Field position after a failed attempt is a key input in fourth-down models.

name: Kneel-Down
short: The quarterback takes the snap and immediately kneels, ending the play so the clock keeps running.
deep: With the opponent out of timeouts, a team can kneel out roughly the final two minutes, since each snap burns up to 40 seconds.
Each kneel loses about a yard but can't be fumbled away easily.
Also used at the end of the first half when a team doesn't want to risk a turnover.

name: Victory Formation
short: The formation used for a kneel-down: tight line, backs behind the quarterback, and a safety deep to guard against a fumble return.
deep: The deep player is there in case a snap is fumbled and the defense tries to return it.
Defenses sometimes rush it, but it's considered poor etiquette and risks injury.
The appearance of this formation usually means the game is over.

name: Hard Count
short: The quarterback uses an exaggerated snap count to try to draw the defense offside, often on 4th-and-short.
deep: If the defense jumps, it's a 5-yard penalty that can give a first down.
Sometimes teams have no intention of snapping; if nobody jumps, they take a delay of game or a timeout.
Offensive linemen must hold still too, or it's a false start.

name: Cadence
short: The quarterback's rhythm of calls before the snap, used to tell teammates when the ball will be snapped.
deep: Varying the cadence keeps pass rushers from timing the snap to get a jump.
In loud road stadiums offenses use a silent count, often a hand signal or head movement, instead of a voice.
A hard count is a cadence designed to draw defenders offside.

name: Green Dot
short: The green sticker on the helmet of the one defensive player allowed a radio to hear the coach's play call.
deep: Only one defender on the field can have the radio, usually a linebacker or safety who relays the call.
The radio cuts off when the play clock hits 15 seconds, so the green-dot player also calls quick adjustments.
The quarterback has the offense's equivalent speaker in his helmet.

name: Mike Point
short: The quarterback or center pointing to one defender and calling him the 'Mike' so the line knows how to set its pass protection.
deep: The Mike in protection terms isn't necessarily the middle linebacker; it's whoever the line designates as its reference point.
Setting the Mike tells each blocker which gap or defender he owns.
Defenses shift late or show double A-gap looks to make the Mike call harder.

name: Run Fit
short: How defenders fill gaps against the run so every gap has someone responsible; a 'bad fit' means a gap was left open.
deep: Each defender has a gap (A, B, C or D) or a force/spill job, and the scheme changes as blockers pull or motion shifts.
Safeties who come down to fill a gap are 'fitting' the run; being late is how runs become long gains.
'Gap integrity' is the same idea: everyone staying in his lane rather than chasing the ball.

name: Spill and Kill
short: A run defense tactic where defenders force the ball carrier to bounce wide, where fast linebackers and safeties are waiting to tackle him.
deep: The spill player attacks the blocker's inside shoulder (often called 'wrong arm') to close the inside lane.
It's the opposite of 'boxing' or setting the edge, where the goal is to keep the ball inside.
Spilling works when your pursuit players are faster than the ball carrier; against a fast back, the edge becomes dangerous.

name: Box Count
short: How many defenders are lined up near the line of scrimmage, inside an area roughly the width of the formation's blockers, ready to stop the run.
watch: Count defenders within about 5-8 yards of the ball and between the tight ends.
deep: Offenses count the box against their blockers: if they have more blockers than defenders, the run is favored.
Typical counts are six or seven; eight or more is 'stacked' or 'loaded'.
Many RPOs are built on the box count: run it if the box is light, throw if it's heavy.

diagram.caption: Seven defenders in the box (highlighted).

name: Loaded Box
short: Eight or more defenders crowding the line of scrimmage to stop the run, usually with one deep safety left.
watch: Count eight defenders near the line with only one safety deep.
deep: It makes running hard but leaves defensive backs in one-on-one coverage behind it.
Offenses respond with play-action and quick outside throws; running backs' efficiency against eight-man boxes is a common stat.
A single-high safety look often comes with a loaded box.

diagram.caption: Eight in the box, one safety deep.

name: Light Box
short: A box with few defenders, usually six or fewer, which invites the offense to run because blockers outnumber or match defenders.
watch: Six defenders near the ball with both safeties deep.
deep: Two-high defenses often play light boxes to protect against the pass, accepting that runs will gain yards.
Offenses with a strong run game punish light boxes and force defenses to bring a safety down.
It's the counterweight of the modern defensive trend toward two-high shells.

diagram.caption: Six in the box vs six blockers: the run looks good.

name: Hands Team
short: The sure-handed players (receivers, tight ends, backs) a team sends out to recover an expected onside kick.
deep: Under current kickoff rules the kicking team must declare an onside attempt, so the hands team knows it's coming.
The goal is simply to secure the ball, not to return it.
Onside kicks rarely succeed under modern rules, so a clean recovery by the hands team usually ends the game.

name: Two-Minute Drill
short: The fast-paced offense a team runs near the end of a half, trying to score while managing the clock and timeouts.
deep: Offenses throw to the sidelines so receivers can step out of bounds and stop the clock.
Spiking the ball stops the clock at the cost of a down.
Defenses often play soft coverage to keep everything in front and make the offense use up time.

name: Four-Minute Offense
short: An offense protecting a late lead runs the ball and stays in bounds to burn clock and end the game.
deep: The goal is first downs, since each one lets the offense bleed another 2-3 minutes.
Defenses respond with loaded boxes and use timeouts right after plays.
A 'four-minute' drive that ends in a kneel-down is considered a well-closed game.

name: Time to Throw
short: How long, on average, a quarterback takes from the snap to the release of his pass.
deep: Under about 2.5 seconds is quick; much longer means deeper drops, longer-developing routes or a quarterback holding the ball.
Short time to throw can hide a weak offensive line; long time to throw invites sacks.
Analysts pair it with pressure rate to judge whether sacks are on the line or the quarterback.

name: Strong Safety
short: The safety who plays closer to the line, usually on the tight end side, and acts like an extra linebacker against the run.
watch: Before the snap, find the safety creeping down toward the linebackers; that is usually the strong safety joining the run defense.
deep: Lines up to the strong side, the side with the tight end, and often walks down into the box late.
Compared with the free safety he tackles more, takes on blockers, and covers tight ends and backs instead of patrolling deep.
Usually the bigger, more physical safety. Range matters less than tackling and nerve in traffic.
Offenses attack him with play-action, hoping he steps up for the run and leaves the area behind him open.
Many modern defenses use interchangeable safeties, so the two labels are less strict than they used to be.

diagram.caption: Strong safety rotating down toward the box.

name: Free Safety
short: The deepest defender, who patrols the middle of the field, reads the quarterback, and stops long passes.
watch: On a deep throw, watch the player arriving from the middle of the field; that is the free safety breaking on the ball.
deep: Called free because he usually has no man to cover and can follow the quarterback's eyes.
Compared with the strong safety he plays deeper, tackles less near the line, and needs more range and ball skills.
Often the lone deep player in Cover 1 and Cover 3, the last line of defense on a breakaway.
Quarterbacks move him with their eyes or a pump fake, then throw to the side he left.
Usually the lighter, faster safety, built more like a cornerback.

diagram.caption: Free safety dropping to the deep middle.

name: Slot Corner
short: A cornerback who covers the slot receiver inside instead of playing out by the sideline.
watch: Find the defensive back lined up inside, across from the slot receiver, and see whether he covers, blitzes, or fills against the run.
deep: In practice this is the same player as the nickelback. Nickelback names the fifth defensive back; slot corner names where he lines up.
Unlike an outside corner he has no sideline to help him, so the receiver can break either way.
Short-area quickness matters more than height or long speed. He also has to tackle, since he sits close to the run.
Defenses blitz him off the slot, and offenses test him with option routes and runs aimed at his side.

diagram.caption: Slot corner carries the slot, or blitzes (dashed).

name: Boundary Corner
short: The cornerback on the short side of the field, the side closer to the sideline when the ball sits on a hash mark.
watch: When the ball is spotted on a hash, the corner on the narrow side is the boundary corner; watch how often he tackles.
deep: With less grass to defend he is closer to the run, so he tackles and takes on blocks more than the field corner.
He often covers the offense's lone receiver to that side, frequently the X, with little safety help.
Usually the bigger, more physical corner who is comfortable in press coverage.
NFL hash marks are narrow, so the difference is smaller than in college. Many NFL teams simply play left and right corners.

diagram.caption: Ball on the left hash: boundary corner on the short side.

name: Field Corner
