short: The cornerback on the wide side of the field, the side with more open grass when the ball sits on a hash mark.
watch: When the ball is on a hash, watch the corner on the wide side; he has far more space to cover.
deep: More room means longer throws and more route options for the receiver, so he needs speed and smooth footwork.
Compared with the boundary corner he is farther from the run and is asked to tackle near the line less often.
Offenses usually put more receivers to the field, so he often works alongside the slot corner and a safety.
NFL hash marks are narrow, so the gap between field and boundary jobs is smaller than in college.

diagram.caption: Ball on the left hash: field corner on the wide side.

name: Will Linebacker
short: The weak side linebacker, who lines up away from the tight end and chases the ball with fewer blockers in his way.
watch: On a run, watch the linebacker on the side without the tight end flow across the field and arrive at the ball.
deep: Will stands for weak side, the side of the formation with fewer blockers.
Defensive linemen are meant to keep blockers off him, so he often leads the team in tackles.
Usually the fastest linebacker. Compared with the Sam he is lighter and plays more in space.
He covers running backs out of the backfield and usually stays on the field in nickel.
Offenses slow him with misdirection, like play-action and counters, that send him the wrong way.

diagram.caption: The Will scrapes across to chase the run.

name: Sam Linebacker
short: The strong side linebacker, who lines up over the tight end, takes on blockers, and holds the edge against the run.
watch: On a run toward the tight end, watch the linebacker on that side meet the block and force the runner back inside.
deep: Sam stands for strong side, the side with the tight end and the extra blocker.
Compared with the Will he is bigger and takes on blocks instead of running free to the ball.
He often covers the tight end, and in some schemes lines up on the line and rushes.
He is usually the linebacker who leaves the field when the defense goes to nickel, so he plays fewer snaps than the others.

diagram.caption: The Sam steps up over the tight end.

name: Three-Technique Tackle
short: The quicker defensive tackle, who lines up on a guard's outside shoulder and tries to shoot the gap into the backfield.
watch: At the snap, watch the tackle between a guard and tackle; if he is in the backfield right away, that is the three-technique at work.
deep: The name comes from his alignment, the 3-technique, on the outside shoulder of a guard.
Unlike a nose tackle, who holds his ground against double teams, his job is to penetrate one gap.
Usually the lighter, quicker tackle, with a fast first step.
He often gets a one-on-one with a guard, which makes him the main inside pass rusher in a four-man front.
Offenses double-team him or run right at him to use his upfield charge against him.

diagram.caption: Three-technique shoots the gap outside the guard.

name: Stand-Up Edge
short: An edge rusher who starts upright in a two-point stance, usually a 3-4 outside linebacker, instead of with a hand on the ground.
watch: Look for the defender standing up at the end of the line; watch whether he rushes the quarterback or drops back into coverage.
deep: A two-point stance means standing on two feet. A defensive end usually puts one hand down in a three-point stance.
Standing up lets him see the backfield, which helps him react to motion and to read the play.
Unlike a hand-down end he is sometimes asked to drop into coverage, which keeps the offense guessing.
Usually lighter and more athletic than a defensive end, and he wins with speed and bend around the tackle.
Offenses run at him or use a tight end to make him prove he can hold the edge.

diagram.caption: Stand-up edge rushing around the left tackle.

name: X Receiver
short: The outside receiver who lines up on the line of scrimmage, usually alone on the side away from the tight end.
watch: Find the receiver standing right on the line, alone on one side; he often gets one-on-one coverage.
deep: Also called the split end. He is on the line, so he cannot go in motion before the snap.
Being on the line means a cornerback can press him at once, so he must beat a jam with strength and technique.
Compared with the Z he gets less help from motion or formation and must win on his own.
Often the biggest, most physical outside receiver, and frequently the top target.
Defenses answer with their best corner or a safety leaning toward his side.

diagram.caption: The X on the line, alone on the left.

name: Z Receiver
short: The outside receiver who lines up a step off the line of scrimmage, usually on the tight end side, and can go in motion.
watch: Look for the outside receiver standing a yard behind the line; he is the one who often goes in motion before the snap.
deep: Also called the flanker. Lining up off the line makes him eligible to move before the snap.
The cushion makes him harder to jam than the X, who is on the line.
Motion lets the offense give him a running start, change the formation, or reveal man or zone coverage.
Often the faster, shiftier outside receiver, used on deep shots, crossing routes, and jet sweeps.

diagram.caption: The Z, off the line, motions inside.

name: H-Back
short: A tight end and fullback hybrid who lines up off the line, just behind the blockers, and moves around to block or catch.
watch: Watch for a tight end standing a step behind the line near the tackle, then crossing the formation at the snap to block.
deep: He lines up off the line of scrimmage, in a wing spot or the backfield, so he can go in motion.
Unlike an in-line tight end he rarely blocks a defensive end head on. He blocks on the move.
Common jobs are leading through a hole like a fullback and cutting off the back side end on split zone.
He also slips into the flat on play-action after faking a block.
Usually shorter and stockier than an in-line tight end, built somewhere between a fullback and a tight end.

diagram.caption: H-back crosses the formation to block the back side.

name: In-Line Tight End
short: A tight end who lines up on the line right next to the offensive tackle and blocks like an extra lineman.
watch: Check the end of the offensive line for a tight end in a three-point stance; see if he blocks or releases into a route.
deep: Often called the Y. He is attached to the formation, on the line beside the tackle.
Compared with a move tight end he blocks defensive ends and linebackers far more often.
Usually the bigger tight end, with the strength to hold up against edge defenders.
Because he really can block, defenses must respect the run, which sets up play-action throws to him.
Tight ends who block and catch at a high level are rare and valuable.

diagram.caption: In-line tight end on the line beside the tackle.

name: Move Tight End
short: A tight end used mostly as a receiver, who lines up in the slot, out wide, or in motion instead of next to the tackle.
watch: Look for a tight end lined up away from the line like a receiver, and note who the defense sends to cover him.
deep: Often called the F. He moves around the formation to find the best matchup.
Compared with an in-line tight end he blocks less and runs many more routes.
Usually lighter and faster, closer to a big receiver than a lineman.
The matchup is the point: too fast for most linebackers, too big for most defensive backs.
Who covers him before the snap, a linebacker or a corner, often tells the quarterback if it is man or zone.

diagram.caption: Move tight end flexed out, motioning back toward the line.

name: Left Tackle
short: The offensive tackle on the left end of the line, who protects a right-handed quarterback's blind side.
watch: On a pass, watch the left end of the line: the tackle slides backward to stay between the edge rusher and the quarterback.
deep: A right-handed quarterback turns his back to the left when he throws, so he cannot see a rusher from that side.
Traditionally the best pass blocker on the line, facing the defense's top edge rusher.
Long arms, quick feet, and balance matter most. He often blocks alone, without a tight end's help.
For a left-handed quarterback the blind side flips, and the right tackle has that job.
Defenses now move their best rushers around, so the gap between left and right tackle has narrowed.

diagram.caption: Left tackle sets back to meet the edge rusher.

name: Right Tackle
short: The offensive tackle on the right end of the line, traditionally the stronger run blocker of the two tackles.
watch: On a run to the right, watch the tackle on that end fire out and try to move the defender in front of him.
deep: A right-handed quarterback can see rushers coming from this side, so the job was long viewed as less risky in pass protection.
Teams often run to the right and put the tight end there, so power and drive blocking are prized.
Compared with the left tackle, the classic right tackle is a bit heavier and a bit less nimble.
That gap has closed. Many top pass rushers now line up over the right tackle, so he must pass block well too.

diagram.caption: Right tackle drives out on the defensive end.

name: Third-Down Back
short: A running back who plays mainly on passing downs because he catches well and can block blitzing defenders.
watch: On third and long, see which running back comes in, then watch whether he stays in to block or slips out for a pass.
deep: His two main jobs are pass protection, picking up blitzers, and running routes out of the backfield.
Compared with an early-down back he carries the ball less and is often smaller and quicker.
He is the usual target on screens, checkdowns, and option routes against linebackers.
Blitz pickup is the hard part. A back who misses his man gets the quarterback hit.
Defenses answer with a faster linebacker or a safety to cover him.

diagram.caption: Third-down back releases into a short route.

name: Dimeback
short: The sixth defensive back, who comes in for a linebacker on obvious passing downs to cover an extra receiver.
watch: On third and long, count the defensive backs; with six on the field, the extra one inside is the dimeback.
deep: Dime is the package with six defensive backs. The nickelback is the fifth, the dimeback the sixth.
He can be a corner or a safety. Teams pick whoever best matches the offense's fourth receiver or tight end.
Coverage ability comes first. With only one linebacker left, the defense is light against the run.
Offenses that see dime may check to a run or a draw to attack the smaller group.

diagram.caption: Dimeback covers the fourth receiver.
